utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Granic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen, please, Exhibit P449. And if we could have page 26 in the Croatian, and page 14 in the English, please. I'm sorry, if we could go forward one page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, there's a paragraph in the -- towards the bottom in the English and at the top in the Croatian. This is a presidential transcript of a meeting on the 18th of August where Mr. Holbrooke, President Tudjman, Ambassador Galbraith, yourself, and others are present. And I'd like to just briefly explore this topic with you. Mr. Holbrooke there on the 18th of August says, towards the middle of that paragraph that one of the things I've said in my presentation was that the US accepts the fact that the Bosnian Serbs should have a separate and parallel relationship with Serbia. This is the change in the US position. This was initially the position held by Alain Juppe. We agree to include this in the future. Therefore, let us agree... with this." And you say -- the president says: "I agree. You say: "Plus a referendum" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The president says: "In two, three, or five years ... possibility. Mr. Holbrooke then says: "A referendum, of course, but the matter of secession and separatism leads to another matter and that is how to implement it. When Czechoslovakia voted to be divided in two, the US and the rest of the world did not say a word. Why? Because this was a fair vote in peace time."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Even in Ethiopia the international community led by the US and UN agreed with the referendum for Eritrea after a specific number of years and Eritrea is now a member of the UN. That is a separate matter. Now, Mr. Granic, to save some time let me see if I understand what is happening here correctly. At this time pursuant to the Washington Agreement, the Muslim Croat Federation already was supposed to have a confederation status with the Republic of Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Croatian Muslim or Croatian Bosniak Federation was created, a confederate agreement was signed between the Federation and the Republic of Croatia. It is true though that not much was done concerning that project because everyone was awaiting the end of the war and the entering of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the final solution for it. This discussion of Mr. Holbrooke with President Tudjman, minister Susak, and myself boils down to the fact that for the first time Mr. Holbrooke said that Americans agreed to it that the same status be accorded to Republika Srpska according to Milosevic's wishes. In other words, for it to establish separate relationship with Serbia. That is it. What I said about the referendum is basically I meant to inquire what exact degree of such relationship they envisaged within the framework of overall relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I understand what Mr. Holbrooke is saying correctly, but you were a participant, you correct me if I'm wrong, get a peace deal signed, the Bosnian Serbs would then be allowed to have a referendum within a certain number of years where they could decide whether they would seek independence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were preliminary discussions in which the possibility of a referendum was not excluded either, as you put it. Later on, when the constitutional principles of the Dayton Accords were laid down, such a referendum was no longer mentioned, much as separation of any particular entity. However, at this point in time, it was still on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go forward a few pages, going to page 17 in the English and page 31 in the Croatian. I'm sorry, if we could go back one page in the English, please -- I mean in the Croatian, please, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And beginning at the paragraph at the bottom where Mr. Holbrooke is speaking in the Croatian version and at the top in the English version. There's a brief recap here by Mr. Holbrooke of the relationship between the United States and Croatia in 1995. He starts off by saying: "I would like to be very honest because our administration has been giving you different signals about military activity in the past months."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Holbrooke continues on in the -- after -- after the president speaks and says: "Mr. President, I want to be absolutely honest with you, speaking not only as a US official but also as a person who cares about this matter, as an individual, as a man who considers himself a friend of Croatia ... that you did much to make a peaceful solution possible and that you had justification for your military operation in Western Slavonia." If you can read to yourself that paragraph, Mr. Granic. But he says -- I'm interested in the following passage. He says: "Then we discussed your activities in Livanjsko Polje and there we again said, 'go ahead'." Now Livanjsko Polje, that refers to the Grahovo and Glamoc operation, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with several operations. There was a number of operations in early 1995. It was known under the name of the Zima 95 or Winter 95 when the Croatian Army was reinforcing its position -- positions. The rest pertains to the Grahovo and Glamoc operations. Both operations went ahead with the approval and understanding of the US. I personally spoke about that with Ambassador Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is what I want to get into because the next sentence I'm interested in. He says: "As you know, we were publicly saying we were concerned but private you knew what we wanted." You were the foreign minister, Mr. Granic. How did President Tudjman know what the United States wanted?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew because we had daily contacts with the most senior officials of the US. I conducted those discussions at the political level as well as Mr. Zuzul. This included state secretary, Mr. Christopher. Then Madeleine Albright who was the special envoy to the UN, and mostly with Mr. Holbrooke during the Washington Agreements, as well as with Mr. Redman and Mr. Gore. Vice-president Gore dealt with the issue when Croatia refused the UN mandate as proposed and another UNCRO mandate was drafted. This happened with the assistance of the US and vice-president Al Gore. In terms of the specific most delicate issues, we always discussed such matters with the special envoy, Mr. Richard Holbrooke. I was personally in charge of that. Although our ambassador to the US, Mr. Zuzul, also conducted such talks. These were diplomatic and political discussions. At the military level this was done by Minister Susak who spoke with Mr. William Perry, the US defence minister. We also had daily contacts with American military representatives in Zagreb. I believe this went on on a daily basis. We also had daily intelligence communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that e-court seems to have gone down in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it -- it gives us some problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technicians are working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There we go. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, he continues on in that paragraph and says: "Then the issue of Knin appeared and the Sector North and South. At that point, we were in a very -- Peter was involved in talks with Babic about the Z-4 plan. There was much confusion. You went ahead. It was a triumph from a political and military point of view" -- and I believe, Mr. President, the sentence should say: "And it used the situation again, it helped again. The only problem are the refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "If could you bring those people back, if could you hold a speech and say that the war is over to return, most of them will not return, but tell them to return, emphasise it, at least mention that they should return." The president then comments: "I would be very content if about 10 percent of them returned. Then Mr. Holbrooke continues: "All right, tell them to return, give them compensation ..." and he goes on. Mr. Granic, as someone who was present at the meeting, can you tell us what you believe or what you understood President Tudjman to mean when he said: "I would be very content if about 10 percent of them returned."

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I thought of it. I believed President firstly believed that there were great many of those who refused to accept Croatia as a state. That there were many insurgent Croatian Serbs who took part in the rebellion. That there were many of them who had committed crimes. One mustn't forget that on the Croatian side, 14.000 soldiers were killed -- sorry, 14.000 people, both civilians and soldiers were killed, and 36.000 were wounded. What President had in mind was also that they were exposed to indoctrination for a number of years and that took its toll as well. I believe that was President's thinking at the time. Perhaps I can add another two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can add what you wish but let me just clarify what my precise question is. Is the President saying here that he would be happy if no more than 10 percent return or that he would be satisfied that up to -- that he could get up do 10 percent to return?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely the latter point. That it would be good if we managed to have 10 percent of them return. His thinking went along those lines, that it would be good if we can manage to have at least 10 percent of them back. I believe some questions will be put to me that will give me an opportunity to explain how the refugee return programme was developed. But these were the President's thoughts at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. We will touch on that topic in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit P463 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a transcript of a conversation between Jure Radic and President Tudjman on the 22nd of August. And I'd like to ask you some questions about that discussion. You -- were you familiar with Jure Radic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me first turn to page 4 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 7 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we scroll down to -- towards the bottom in the Croatian and in the English, Dr. Radic is talking about the problem of burning that's taking place, and he says: "However, one thing I have to tell you is that I visited all this now both by car and by helicopter." The translation here is -- in English is: "Our men torched a lot. They're torching today as they did yesterday, president, it's no good."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "I went to Kijevo to see, I know that area very well. There is a village of Civljane near Kijevo of equal size, a Serb village where they renewed nice houses and told them everything has been preserved. I got there on the day of assumption of the Virgin Mary to find everything has been burned down. Not in the cities, because the authorities were obviously more powerful there, but in the villages. It is not the army, it's the fifth echelon which is under, I don't know whose, what kind of banner, put on a uniform, wander about, those are the worst tramps torching and looting around. That is our property. It's not someone else's. What if he burned down the Serb village near Kijevo where we could accommodate our population?" The last sentence in that entry is: "I'm not telling you hearsay but things I've experienced myself and seen with my own eyes, torching and looting." And the president says: "So we said military police right away and civilian police right after that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please, in Croatian. Actually, if we could go to page 7 in the English, which is page 10 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The conversation continues on that topic -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, page 11; if we could go forward one page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The last sentence there where -- in an entry where Mr. Radic says: "We have to organise ourselves somehow in order to prevent this. The president says: "We talked about preventing this from the beginning." Radic says: "We did, everybody's referring to you in a positive context and everybody's referring to you of all the people because you were saying that we shouldn't do that. But that hasn't been implemented. We have to go for VONS or somewhere, let people speak and submit a report on that. Here, I am, all the county executives are telling me about that, all of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please, and turn the page in Croatian as well. And towards the bottom in Croatian and in the middle in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Radic continues and says: "So, if we have to introduce order anywhere in this area, almost a despotism in a way in the beginning we cannot be without that, because there has to be a boss, one must know who gives orders in each of these segments, and a hierarchy should be established in the authority from the above, regarding colonising and regarding living over there." The president says: "That's what I say. That's in all wars. If we didn't abolish the death penalty for robbery, the Court would shoot them." And then Radic says: "But we should catch them, some of them now and prevent that because of the relationship with the world and ourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English and Croatian. Towards the bottom. That's it. If we could turn the page, I'm sorry, in Croatian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Radic says: "They're probably revenging but he cannot get in there because the police control him. So he puts on a military uniform, because now everybody wears a military uniform. Everybody is walking around the city in them, even those who have never been to the army. I think it's primarily" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please -- sorry, back one page in Croatian. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "I think it's primarily the ones who have never even been to the army, the ones who drag that, rob, take away, et cetera." Now, Mr. Granic, this is a private conversation between Mr. Radic and President Tudjman. The description here by Mr. Radic about what is going on on the ground first and foremost that it's not the army, it's people putting on uniforms and going in, people avenging themselves, is that, at that time what you also had understood to be the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Of course, this is a private conversation between Minister Radic and President Tudjman. But a day or two later, he repeated that at a meeting of their Croatian cabinets, and my personal position and the position of the government was the same. These were criminals, criminals who were torching and looting, most often dressed in uniform. And, generally speaking, in wartime, in those areas, people who had never been to the army or in the police were wearing uniforms. And especially in these situations, because it was easier for them to gain access to various places on the ground, and do their dirty business, therefore, I too, understood that these were criminals, that they were criminal groups very often dressed in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you noted -- you note -- you should note that the president there says: "We talked about stopping this -- preventing this from the beginning." He also says: "So we said military police right away and civil police right after that." Was it your understanding before Operation Storm that the president had issued orders to prevent such criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, before Operation Storm, already before the 31st of July during the Brioni meeting between the head of state with the top military leadership, I was asked by the president to provide a political and diplomatic appraisal of the military operation. I told the President that in view of the situation in Bihac, in view of the threats by Martic and Karadzic about the creation of a joint state, in view of all of the international circumstances, I said that we would get through the Security Council only with a presidential statement because our military operation fit into the US initiative. But I also told the President that the most important thing is to comply with the Geneva Conventions, to comply with our obligations towards the UNCRO soldiers and protect them, to make the operation clean, and to make it as short as possible. The president then told me that he would do his utmost to respect the civilians, UNCRO soldiers, and all the property. I know that he made -- gave instructions accordingly to Minister Jarnjak because Minister Jarnjak spoke about this on the first day of Operation Storm. Therefore, the President did issue that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue on with this transcript, Mr. Granic, because there's another topic that then begins on that same page. And within that same paragraph that we just finished talking about, Mr. Radic starts a discussion and it says: "Now look, have I been looking around this area a bit, the biggest centres where we should focus on return regarding the national interest. I have tried to make a chronological order or some kind of hierarchy and in my opinion I would like to discuss this with you a bit." "The map of the whole area is of strategic importance for Croatia. I coloured it with different colours. This is what has always been critical for us in the history, not Knin, who managed to do that slowly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "If you ask me, the first I define the five priorities" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could change the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "According to the urgency of colonising these places with Croats. "If you ask me, this thing right here is the first and the second priority. We should bring Croats back here urgently, and this area should be urgently colonised with Croats, and we should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again. Because, that's where we were cut off." The president says: "Not even 10 percent." Radic continues: "Okay. I am talking about 10 per cent. So the first priority of colonising is this right here. In my opinion, Petrova and Zrinska Gora, that's where we have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later. We also have Vojnic and Veljun, a somewhat smaller place, but Vojnic is a bigger place. "However, by our company's opening factories just as the Serbs did in Licki Osijek..." and he goes on. Now, Mr. Granic, it appears that they're looking at a map when they're having this discussion, and Radic talks about settling Croats in the area that they're looking at, and there's a reference to Petrova and Zrinska Gora where we were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, I would like to pull up a map. It's 65 ter 1D3011.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, Mr. Granic, I would like to have you assist the Court in locating the places that Mr. Radic is talking about here. Now, Mr. Granic, the red line there represents what the RSK actually controlled. The blue line is what they declared should be under their control. With a -- the usher will provide you a blue pen and you can mark on the screen. But can you show the Court where Petrova and Zrinska Gora are as well as Vojnic. If you could circle the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in a little bit on the map. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you -- can you circle on the screen, draw a circle around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, can we zoom in a little bit on the map so we can see the names of the counties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but once zoomed in and marked, we can't change the zoom level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just a little bit. If we can move the map down a little bit. There we go, and zoom in the upper -- there we go. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that help you see a little bit better?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This. This is it Vojnic. Vrginmost, Slunj. That's the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle. You can touch the screen. Don't worry about touching the screen. Drawn on it, draw a circle around that area.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in fact, Mr. Granic, the RSK right there, when Radic talks about "that's where we were cut off," that was the shortest or the place where Croatia was actually in the most danger because of the short distance or the short amount of the territory that it controlled there, correct? It's about 20 kilometres wide in terms of what Croatia held between 1991 and 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, is Mr. Radic here talking about keeping Serbs from coming back into the area or moving Croats in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We know that Dr. Granic didn't attend at this meeting. I object to him speculating of what Mr. Radic or Tudjman meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, he should be rather cautious, but earlier Mr. Granic has already told us that what the thoughts of the President, of President Tudjman were. Of course, we'll understand this as the interpretation by someone who was acquainted with the situation at the time, what his interpretation is. Whether that interpretation is right or wrong, Mr. Waespi, is -- is still to be determined, just as it has to be determined on the basis of what skills, Mr. Granic, even be a medical doctor knows what the thoughts of a person are but rather how he interprets the words of those persons. That has been done several times by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and the limits and the evidentiary, the probative value of these interpretations is for the Chamber finally to make. Therefore, I'm not -- stop Mr. Misetic at the time. At the same time, I don't think that Mr. Granic would disagree with me that no one can know what someone else's thoughts are, although you sometimes can form an opinion about what you think someone else thinks. I take it, Mr. Granic, that you understood that, and in this context, at the same time it has been done several times, let's not spend too much time on the interpretation of words, which sometimes, and I'm referring to some of the words we looked at earlier, the 10 per cent, for example, which we have looked at already many, many times and of which we know exactly what the interpretation from one side is and what the interpretation from the other side is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just -- I appreciate and I'll move forward; however, at the end of the day the Prosecution wasn't at the meeting either nor was I, but we're going to be arguing about how to interpret this text, and to that extent since Mr. Granic was virtually at the top of the state at the time, he may have some additional insight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you're also aware that the position of a witness is not the same as the position of counsel arguing. We do not expect, as a matter of fact, witnesses to argue but rather to tell us what they know. So, therefore, that you and Mr. Waespi will do it, of course, is only of little relevance for what we expect the witness to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, is this a discussion about keeping Serbs out of Croatia or moving Croats in to that area that you have circled on the map?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I agree with what the Prosecutor says. Of course, I wasn't there. Your Honours, I don't want to go into what Radic might have thought, but I know what the positions of Radic were in his capacity as a minister for reconstruction and a minister who was also in charge of demography. His objective was to resettle as many Croats as possible into that empty area. By no means was his intention to prevent Serbs from returning. First of all, Jure Radic did not work for that, and I expect I'll have a lot more to say today about all the work that had been done for the return of Serbs, because I was involved in that. But as for Croats -- as far as Croats are concerned, Mr. Tudjman had created a ministry for returnees in Croatia, and the intention was for as many Croats to be resettled into areas that were virtually empty. Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina or anywhere from all over the world. However, this failed. Only a small number of Croats who been expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina remained in that territory. The objectives were much higher but only a minimal number of Croats compelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina remained in that area and very few Croats from other countries were resettled there. Most of them stayed in big cities. Most of the Croats expelled from Republika Srpska and other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina stayed in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the map on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I get some foundational material on what these borders represent, where they are from, perhaps other maps that are already admitted before I say anything about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's directly from the book of maps provided by the Prosecution at the beginning in the opening statements, and the legend is at the bottom left-hand portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which map of the booklet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At this point I don't know which number it is, but there's an ERN number at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I can imagine that you want to verify whether Mr. Misetic rightly said that this is a map from the booklet. He is smart enough not to take any risk in this respect. But then it comes as a surprise that it is your own material, but please tell me what the page is, is really not something that -- as far as I'm concerned please verify whether Mr. Misetic is correct. Then the page is certainly something you could agree upon during a break and a conversation of -- well, half a minute or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised it is map 4 in the book of maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the map says itself, as a matter of fact, that my eyes are not ... Map 4, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could get a number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become Exhibit number D1817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, some of these maps have been admitted per agreement among the parties, and I'm not sure whether this one is among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no recollection either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not. Then -- may I then take it, after some inquiries but without having expressed whether you have any objections, that there are no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1817 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if could have Exhibit P891 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I'm going to now discuss with you a little about some correspondence from Foreign Minister Kinkel to you in the third week of August and your response to him. And the first is going to be an ECMM report, if we could look in the middle of that page. It says: "The German foreign minister -- and if we have -- there we go. It says: "The German foreign minister Klaus Kinkel has sent a letter to his Croatian counterpart Mate Granic expressing his concern about the Croatian behaviour towards Serbs and Serb property. According to the Zagreb newspaper "Vjesnik," Dr. Granic was surprised and blamed exaggerated or even biased reports for causing Mr. Kinkel's reaction." And there's a comment by the ECMM observer. "One has to admire the stamina with which somehow --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "One has to admire the stamina with which some politicians are able to stick to their own fabricated lies."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to 65 ter 1D3005, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a media report from the Croatian news agency which carried your letter in response to Foreign Minister Kinkel, and I would like to go over that with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the first paragraph towards the upper middle portion, it says: "Minister Granic responded that he received the letter with understanding but that he is also surprised because it is apparent that Minister Kinkel's reactions are based on reports which are exaggerated or even deliberately tendentious. Dr. Granic reminded Minister Kinkel that the UN information and political office in Zagreb stated that they had exaggerated in their reports even during the liberation of Western Slavonia in order to prevent the Croats in advance from committing crimes, and for politically recognisable but however morally unacceptable reasons certain international observers continued with this type of practice after the latest joint operation carried out by the Croatian military and police ... "Minister Granic emphasised in his letter how he does not wish to dissuade his German colleague regarding individual incidents which in most cases were committed by vengeful or reckless individuals and most often those whose own property in many settlements has been entirely destroyed. "Dr. Granic also noted that these individual incidents, taking into account the size of the area, are in reality small in number, and added that regardless of some past negative experiences regarding the objectivity of their reporting, representatives of the UN, EU, and humanitarian organisations will keep having full freedom of movement in the liberated area." Now, we can stop right there for a moment. Can you explain to the Court when you wrote to Minister Kinkel on the 25th of August, what your thoughts were concerning exaggerated or even deliberately tendentious reports and how that was connected to your experience in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from this letter that I had received from Minister Kinkel, at that time, I spoke to him at least five or six times on the telephone. Minister Kinkel was a man of high moral fiber, very sensitive to any human rights violations, and we had a completely open and frank relationship which was tainted by certain exaggerations in the beginning that we had compelled Croatian Serbs. And I was especially sensitive to that, because even if we had wanted to, we could not keep them from leaving. 130 to 140.000 Serbs left during and after Operation Storm. Another thing I was sensitive to, or about, was that Knin had been destroyed due to excessive and undiscriminating shelling which according to all my knowledge was not true. I was also sensitive to the scale of problems that occurred involving looting, torching, et cetera. The UN reports at that time reported accurately. The problem gave cause for concern, but it was not as widespread as certain individuals and media throughout the world claimed. I understood this as an impetus by which I mean that after this letter, and after the phone call made by Chancellor Kohl to President Tudjman which Kinkel and I also discussed, to encourage anyone who had any power in Croatia to do their utmost at the level of the foreign minister, the minister of defence, the government, President Tudjman, they all were encouraged to do their utmost to stop this. And there was a special session of the cabinet devoted to that. I called one reporter from the weekly Globus to tell him all this and to tell him also that this should be given a broad and accurate coverage without hiding anything. I also said that an agreement had been reached within the government and with the president that all international institutions that want to be represented on the ground in order to report should be allowed to. The UN, the UNCRO, Helsinki Watch, the European Union, embassies and their military attaches. They were already all on the ground. Later, we allowed the permanent mission of the OSCE and a temporary mission before that. And I want to emphasise on thing, it was one thing after Operation Flash when there was really no serious human rights violations and quite another -- and another thing after my meeting in Geneva on the 6th of August when Reuters reported on that meeting, regardless of the fact that I gave a press conference for 200 journalists, and still the reporting did not reflect what I said at the time meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Misetic, page 21, line 20, the witness referred to a specific person or office when he talked about a report, so I -- I don't think that was specifically clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to make the same comment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Granic, you said the following, and those who can follow you in your own language said that not every detail was transcribed and translated for us. You said: "I was also sensitive to the scale of problems that occurred involving looting, torching, et cetera. The UN reports at that time reported accurately. The problem gave cause for concern but it was not as widespread as certain individuals and media throughout the world claimed." Now, some have heard that you referred to a specific person. If that's correct, could you please repeat to what person you referred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no one in particular. I had in mind those who reported wrongly. I did not single out a particular medium or person. I did use an example, however, when I said that the Reuters wrongly reported after my meeting in Geneva with Javier Solana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He's focusing on the wrong sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think under these circumstances we would allow you to see whether what you had is in line with what Mr. Granic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, the sentence in English was interpreted as "the UN reports at the time reported accurately." I guess I'll just -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the report of the Secretary-General of the UN, Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, this is what I referred to. It was a balanced report and that it reflected correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you start expanding on the report, we just wanted to check the transcript and you refer to the Secretary-General and not to the United Nations as a body. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the report in a few minutes, Mr. Granic. But let me finish with this --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll -- let's me finish with this reply to Minister Kinkel. Towards the bottom in English, you say: "Croatia most certainly wishes and has an interest in preserving the remaining property in these areas because it is also part of the wealth of the Republic of Croatia regardless of the ethnic or other kind of origin of the owner of the property." Then the next paragraph on the issue of returns says: "When talking about the return of those Croatian Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Who left to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that is Serbia or Montenegro, or parts of Bosnia, continued Minister Granic, the Croatian government is taking all possible measures to organise the return well which will take a certain amount of time and the co-operation of international humanitarian organisations but also the willingness of the authorities in Belgrade which are currently forcibly mobilising a significant part of the newly arrived people and are sending them to the army of the Bosnian Serbs, and Croatia cannot be held responsible for these kinds of injustices and consequences." Mr. Granic, that was your comment to -- or your letter to Minister Kinkel. Explain to the Chamber how the issue of mobilisation of Croatian Serbs into the army of the Bosnian Serbs impacted the issue of the return of Croatian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a very negative impact. In general, a refugee return project is a very serious and comprehensive project which cannot be undertaken without the UNHCR. The UNHCR laid down some rules first and foremost out of security and safety. However, as the refugees from Croatia were being recruited and sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina to join the army of Republika Srpska, and as there were threats of terrorist activities, this made us all the more wary, and at that time there were no preconditions to put together a return programme. This is what the UNHCR fully agreed with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. Was there any concern about the danger of bringing in people who might be -- who might still be combatants?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there was. We had to bear in mind that we were still in a state of war with the FRY, and that parts of their army were in our territory in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. There were daily provocations from Republika Srpska towards Croatia. At that time, the idea of a FRY military intervention against Croatia was still something that was being contemplated to an extent. All these things had to be borne in mind. When I say all this, I say it on the basis of all the intelligence data we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit number D1818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Granic, may I seek clarification of your last answer. You said you had to bear in mind that you were still in a state of war and that parts of "their army" were on your territory in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja and then you continued about the provocations. Were such provocations also -- took also place in the Krajina, because you specifically referred to Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. What you said after that, would that apply both to the Krajina and Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, or were you mainly focussing on Eastern Slavonia and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, I focused on Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, the area of Slavonski Brod and Zupanja. These were the areas that I had in mind when I referred to the provocations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, yesterday we saw Exhibit D1816 which was the transcript of the conversation between President Tudjman and Chancellor Kohl. You have now mentioned that you felt that Secretary-General Ghali's report was something to the effect that it was reasonable. President Tudjman on that conversation with Chancellor Kohl also referenced the Ghali report as a more reasonable assessment of the situation. I would like to take a look at that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, first, before we do that, if I could take a look at 65 ter 1D3009 which is another presidential transcript of a meeting where you are present. And in the Croatian version, it begins at page 30. Now this we did -- a relevant excerpt has been translated here in English. Page 4 in e-court of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The conversation, Dr. Granic, is about -- this is now -- the date is the 9th of September and the conversation is about the fact that you had received a rather sharp note from Minister Kinkel while President Tudjman had received around the same time a conversation from Chancellor Kohl and so the -- you and Mr. Zuzul, Mr. Sarinic, and President Tudjman are discussing how to interpret the two messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please. Sorry, sorry, if we could stay on the page. I'm sorry, page 2. It is page 2, I apologise. Yes, the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the top, Mr. Zuzul says: "The other matter, Steinar told me while still in Paris, something like, speaking as a friend and in private, something about Kinkel being angry at me, and then at you, at us, but also at me, because I allegedly went there to, how they understood it, to complain to Kohl about that letter because it says there in the note, because he told me, neither do they know about Kinkel's letter to Granic nor do they support it, and they particularly do not support the fact that the letter appeared in the newspapers because it's not their style." Towards the middle of the page in English. "Because Kohl called Kinkel, maybe it's difficult to say, to account for it, but in any case, Kohl called Kinkel and pointed out to him the difference in conduct towards Croatia from his side and from the side of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs." And then the bottom of the page in English, if we can scroll down in Croatian, Mr. Zuzul again continues -- Yes. "I said, according to instructions by the President that we feel that the spirit of communication is different when, Kohl's letter on one side, Kohl's telephone call to the President, and Kinkel's letter on the other side, entirely different and with Minister Susak, also different ..." Now, can you explain, Mr. Granic, what was transpiring there and how the Croatian -- you in the Croatian foreign ministry and Mr. Zuzul were interpreting what was taking place between Chancellor Kohl and Minister Kinkel in terms of their policy towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of Chancellor Kohl was definitely the official position of Germany on the situation in Croatian at the moment. However, regarding Minister Kinkel, he was always a bit more temperamental. He told me clearly that frequently even concerning small issues he was put under pressure by other colleagues from the European Union, especially the UK, and he always overreacted to many things. But personally I never held it against him, because I was absolutely certain that he did it with the best of intentions. This only served as an incentive for me to try and do our utmost to stop the evil that was taking place in the liberated area. As a minister though I had to respond in terms of the facts. I had my disposal which I had received from our services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D3009 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1819.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1819 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I would like to turn now to the Ghali report, the Secretary-General's report of the 23rd of August, which is Exhibit D90. Again this is a report referenced by you today in your testimony and by President Tudjman in his conversation with Chancellor Kohl.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have page 5 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the report about the situation in Croatia. And the relevant portions concerning the situation on the ground in terms of burning, looting, and other criminal activities that were taking place are paragraphs 17 to 19 of the report. If you could read through that to save me having to read all of it. But it talks about a certain number of houses having been noticed to have been burning. 35 to 40 houses in one stretch. One house in Topusko. Reports of -- a few reports of physical violence. Paragraph 19 talks about how the ICRC reported favourably on the access they have been given to all persons detained. Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to 65 ter 1D3010, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is the assessment of the Croatian mission to the UN in New York. The internal assessment that was sent to you in terms of interpreting the Secretary-General's report. It's dated the 24th of August. It was sent to the President and to you, amongst others. Second paragraph says: "The report can be divided into two parts. The first part relates to the assessment of the consequences of Operation Storm (with certain notes on its course) with special emphasis on the humanitarian situation ..." The next paragraph says: "The report can in its entirety be assessed as positive and favourable for the Republic of Croatia despite some negative tones entailed in the first part of the document (this involves certain negative assessments of Croatia's relation toward Serb refugees and their property as well as jeopardising the safety of UNCRO). "It is indicative that there is not a single sentence in this report which would dispute the political and legal framework of Storm. On the contrary, Ghali's report is written in the manner which fully accepts and protects..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia within its internationally recognised borders."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please, and go to paragraph numbered 6 in the Croatia, which is page 3. "The assessment was the part of the report that relates to the assessments of the humanitarian situation as well as the occurrences during Storm is in most part written correctly with a clearly notable aspiration of the UN secretariat to be objective in their actions and avoid any kind of political assessments of events." The next paragraph: "We would like to turn the attention to paragraphs 17, 18, and 19 of the report, which even though they contain some negative assessments against the Republic of Croatia, in principle show that the degree and extent of destruction in the liberated territories as a consequence of Storm are substantially smaller than what some earlier assessments by UN observers indicated. When discussing the mass flight of Serbs, emphasis is made in the report that it is 'difficult to assess to what extent the mass exodus of the population of the Krajina Serbs was the result of fear of the Croatian forces and the refusal to live under Croatian authority, or a result of the encouragements to flee by the local leaders.' This removes any possibility of further accusations against the Republic of Croatia for the alleged deportations of Serbs, or, rather, it closes the window for malicious interpretations of the reasons of the Serb flight." And it is signed by Vladimir Drobnjak and the Ambassador Mario Nobilo, Croatia's ambassador in New York. Mr. Granic, two-part question: First, was this assessment of Secretary-General Ghali's report something you relied on in drafting your reports to Minister Kinkel as well as to the - and we'll look at it later - the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr. Lasso-Ayala. Is the Secretary-General's assessment and -- this assessment of the Secretary-General's report something you relied on?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As a foreign minister, I accepted this assessment. The President himself also received it, and we discussed it. We concluded that the report and the assessment were fully acceptable to us, and that is should serve as an impetus to actively stop the events mentioned in paragraphs 17, 18 and 19, that is to say, the events in the field. There was a very clear assessment of the reasons why the Croatian Serbs left the occupied areas. It did -- the report does not question the legitimacy of our operation. One needs to mention that the General Assembly of the UN in December 1995 issued a resolution number 43/49 on the situation in the liberated areas of Croatia whereby the territory was proclaimed part -- part of Croatia and Belgrade was singled out as the one instance that was responsible for the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you and President Tudjman, as far as you know, consider the Secretary-General's report to be more objective than the reports being circulated by the ECMM and the UN teams on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly put, we believed it was the most objective and the best assessment at the moment of the situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and I'm about to shift topics, so it might be a good time for a break. I'm sorry, and I also have to tender the exhibit which is 65 ter 1D3010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. We will have a break, and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just at the outset I wish to alert the Chamber that Mr. Kay and I have had a discussion, and Mr. Kay will not be cross-examining and so I have -- he is graciously allowed me to use the balance of his time, and I have spoken with Mr. Waespi and unless I finish early, Mr. Waespi is prepared to begin at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood, and the Chamber appreciates the co-operation between the parties in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I'd like to turn your attention now to Exhibit P641. Mr. Granic, this is a letter from the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr. Jose Ayala-Lasso and it was sent to President Tudjman on the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in it, in the fourth paragraph, if we turn the page in English, please, and in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph he says: "In this respect, it has been brought to my attention that an extensive wave of looting of the property belonging to the local Serbs took place immediately after the fighting had stopped and the Croatian forces had entered into the region of Krajina. There also appears to be a systematic burning of houses and fields, particularly in the southern part of the region. Fires of evident deliberate origin after the fighting was over have reportedly resulted in the destruction of practically entire towns, such as Kistanje, Djevrska, Otric, and Donji Lapac. This continues even to the present date."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Moreover Croatian military personnel have been observed where the fires have occurred in some confirmed instances with large cannisters, fire access and similar equipment. And Croatian police and other authorities have been seen passing these locations without taking any apparent steps to stop them." And now, Mr. Granic, I would like to show you Exhibit P642, which is a letter you prepared to the High Commissioner for Human Rights in response this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph, you write: "First of all, let me reiterate that the President of the Republic, his excellency Dr. Franjo Tudjman, thoroughly rejected allegations in regard to the suspected systematic burning and looting of houses and fields in the recently liberated territories during his press conference on 18 August 1995, where he stated, inter alia, that 'the Croatian Army did not undertake any actions of burning and looting anywhere ... Croatian authorities, myself personally and the Croatian government did everything within their power to prevent the suffering of civilians and damage to civilian structures to the greatest extent possible'."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You continued: "As you will recall, during the preparations and execution of the Croatian Army and police operation to recover its occupied territories, Croatian troops were under explicit orders to ensure that human casualties and material damages to property be limited to the absolute minimum. Notwithstanding this as well as taking into consideration the scope of the recent operation, it is possible that some incidents of which you refer to in your letter occurred. Moreover, it is possible that in accordance with the evacuation orders issued by the local Serb leadership, incidents such as these could have been committed by the retreating Serbs themselves. "I assure you that all alleged incidents will be investigated by the competent authorities of the Republic of Croatia and that the results of these investigations will become public in due time. In addition, I can further assure that you the Croatian government has taken all the necessary measures to prevent any further incidents from occurring." Now, Minister Granic, I'd like to ask you, the first part I read out and the second part, compared to the second part were you saying that there were no incidents at all of the Croatian Army making any -- committing any crime or, in reading that second paragraph, were you saying that despite orders that were given it is possible that some of these incidents did occur, during the operation itself?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent this letter at the request of the President. Before that, of course, I had received information from the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence. At that time, we did not have information that the army was committing any kind of crimes, none whatsoever. But we not only understood this letter seriously but after the letter of Minister Kinkel, we had a special open session of the cabinet, where we discussed openly and condemned seriously all incidents of looting, torching, and individual killings. That's all we had in terms of information at the time, and we spoke about it publicly, but we did not have information that all this was being done by either the army or the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You don't exclude, however, the possibility that in fact there may have been some incidents of looting or burning that took place during or immediately after Operation Storm, by some members of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. No reasonable person can claim that such things cannot happen when 200.000 soldiers were on the move. However, we did not have any such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, when you say: "We did not have any such reports, are you referring to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The foreign ministry received reports exclusively through official channels, from the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, plus, at the time, we had a vice prime minister for humanitarian issues, Dr. Ivica Kostovic, who was a man of great integrity, and his job was mainly to collect information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have Exhibit P918 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Minister Granic, this is a -- a warning that was sent by the political affairs department of The Ministry of Defence within the Croatian Army. If you look at the second paragraph, it says: "However, because of the irresponsibility of individual soldiers, non-commissioned officers and officers, who compromise the Croatian Army and state through their inappropriate conduct and acts, this success has been partly brought into question. As a result of the above, the possibility exists that the international community could undertake measures which would have unforeseeable consequences for our state. "For this reason, the following -- and following the policy of the Supreme Commander, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, as well as the instructions of the defence minister and the political administration of the defence ministry of the Republic of Croatia, it is necessary to immediately prevent the following: "1, the continued torching and destruction of facilities and property throughout the entire liberated territory; 2, the killing of livestock; 3, the confiscation of property; 4, inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war, and especially towards members and soldiers of the peace forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This was within the Ministry of Defence, Minister Granic, and it seems to make reference to some incidents that occurred due to the irresponsibility of individual soldiers, NCOs, and officers. Were you aware of this at the time, or was this type of information delivered to you in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in political talks before this dispatch was sent. I did not have this report but I knew this was going to be sent because it was the result of talks at the top political level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this question: Mr. Granic, we've seen now through the course of the morning that there were discussions between minister Radic and President Tudjman about the fifth echelon and not the regular army committing these crimes. Yesterday you were shown by Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I have a problem as a non-native speaker, although I understand fifth echelon, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Text used in this conversation so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we could ask the witness: What did you understand the fifth echelon to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminals dressed in military uniform. That's how I understood it. Criminal groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I do not know whether you have done with the previous document. I was just asking myself what evidence this Chamber received. Mr. Granic, this letter was put to you in which there was a certain -- not any person of the armed forces participated in that. I don't know whether you were going to give that a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I will wait and see what happens. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, my question was going to be, if in fact within the Ministry of Defence they had recognised that there was at least some problem with respect to this, what was the reason that you would have written to the High Commissioner of Human Rights on the 23rd of August to say that the Croatian Army -- if I can quote it, essentially that the Croatian Army did not commit any criminal acts anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote exclusively based on information I would get in writing from the defence ministry, from the interior ministry, and it was on that basis that I always wrote my reports. The foreign ministry did not have any special service to deal with this. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, did you receive any written report that the Croatian Army did not undertake any actions of burning and looting anywhere? Did you receive that in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did receive information from other sources that such things, too, were happening, as individual incidents, and I always vehemently reacted. I informed the President, the minister of Defence and the prime minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not an answer to my question. You write or it was written that "the Croatian Army did not undertake any actions of burning and looting anywhere." Now, when asked why you wrote that, you said, I would base, we had no -- we had no facilities to do our own research so I would rely on written reports we received. Now, my question is: Did you receive a written report which said that the Croatian Army did not undertake any actions of burning and looting anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, Your Honours, at the time when I was writing this report, I had no information that the Croatian Army was responsible for any such crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, that was not my question. You say, In my communications, I would rely exclusively on written official reports we received. Now, from your answer I still have not heard that what seems to be a firm denial of any involvement of any army member, I have not heard you to say that this was based on written official reports you had received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. My answer was based on the written reports I got from the interior ministry and the defence ministry. I did not receive reports saying that the army had committed a crime of the kind that I discussed in my letter to Mr. Lasso-Alaya. I did not receive such reports from the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I take it that you see the difference between saying, I never received any report confirming your allegations; and no member of the army anywhere ever did commit such crimes. The one is a statement about that you have not received any information from your own services which could confirm the allegations. The other one is a flat denial of such allegations. Not to say, I've not seen any evidence; but it did not happen. There is a difference between the two, and I'm drawing your attention to this difference, so that if you want, that you can make any comments or observations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I can, Your Honour. Your observation was quite correct. I cannot say it's quite certain that no member ever committed a dishonourable act. I mean, member of the Croatian armed forces. Even in this paper called "warning," we read that some people did concern things. However, at the moment when I was writing, I did not have any written reports that a member of the Croatian forces was responsible for any such things. But, of course, I cannot deny the possibility that some did, and that's why I wrote what I wrote to Mr. Lasso-Ayala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just follow up, Mr. Granic. If you look back at the paragraph on your screen -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go back to your letter, which is P642, please. If we could go to page 2 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The letter actually it says that you're quoting from the press conference of the President on the 18th of August, not that you're quoting from some report that you received. So the comment is actually a quote from President Tudjman's press conference on the 18th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had to invoke the words of the President on one occasion because the letter was one thing and another thing was the press conference given by the President. And, of course, yet another thing, was that I received information as the foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And as someone who worked closely with the President, at that time, and he says that the allegation -- he rejected -- the President rejected the allegation of systematic burning and looting of houses and fields, does this denial relate to what we talked about yesterday, Croatia's concern about how such allegations would impact its ability to get the US support for operations in western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. It was very painful for us whenever we received such reports. They not only undermined the credibility of Croatia and us all, they undermined the future of Croatia and the upcoming operations in Bosnia and the future peace in Bosnia. It reduced the chances of peaceful co-operation, and the people who were responsible for this were working against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned I think, peaceful reintegration. You're referring to the reduced Croatia's position in terms of the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. That's what you're referring to, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I meant peaceful reintegration in Eastern Slavonia. Because, as soon as Operation Storm ended, talks with the US began already on the 18th, during the visit of Ambassador Holbrooke to Zagreb. We started talks about how to peacefully reintegrate Eastern Slavonia Baranja and Baranja as well into the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I would like to turn your attention to Exhibit P466, please. And this is a presidential transcript from the 30th of August. You are present during this meeting as was Minister Jarnjak and President Tudjman, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 55 in the B/C/S, and page 26 in the English, please. Yes, I'm sorry, if we could go one page back in the B/C/S. Page 53 -- sorry, page 53. I'm sorry, one more page back. Page 53 in e-court. That's it. If we can go back one page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look on the bottom of your page, Mr. Granic, when Mr. Jarnjak begins to speak, and it's at the top of the English, Mr. Jarnjak says: "And I should mention the other question that became operational now, and I have to say it is not a big one, but it appears. The question is about the Serbs that are coming through Hungary and they are coming to knock on our border, because they want to come back." The President says: "Do they have our passports?" Mr. Jarnjak says: "No they do not have anything. Mr. Sarinic says: "They have Yugoslav passports. Mr. Jarnjak says: "I would like us to give them instructions that they should get entry visas in Belgrade in our office, if you agree." The President says: "I would not give anything. You have to give instructions to the customs that they should not let people without papers to cross border." Mr. Sarinic then comments: "President let us get inspired the way it is in western Slavonia. It is very positive for us, because no one came back. Let them report to the international humanitarian organisations and then those organisations should give us ..." And then the president says: "Wait a second, he comes" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "He comes from another country and the customs officer does not conduct any politics."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, please, and scroll down in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a comment attributed to you which says: "According to the agreement in Belgrade, there are only 204 of them that are registered, and they started to register in Skopje, so they did that as well down there. And the third thing is that they started to come here without any papers." The President says: "If we let 204 persons come here now [sic] tomorrow you would have 1204 and in ten days 12.000. Nothing for now." Mr. Granic, can you explain your understanding of that context as well as your comments on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain both things. At that time, there were absolutely no preconditions that were put in place for any refugee return. At that time, there was a possible military intervention of the FRY against Croatia still suspended somewhere in mid-air. It was the time when the government of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina in exile was formed. At that time, there were -- there was a threat of terrorist attacks against Croatia. At that time, some of the refugees were being recruited into the army of Republika Srpska. It is true that a plan for refugee return can only be put together with the assistance of the international community. I reported on the 204 applications in Belgrade in our office. At that time, we still did not have diplomatic relations established. Thus, we had only an office instead of a mission. I reported of the 204 persons who appeared there with our documents. At that point in time, there was no other way to treat this, save for allowing individual arrivals or family reunions. I personally did as follows: Firstly, in Dayton, by the Erdut Agreement, the issue of Eastern Slavonia and the process of peaceful reintegration was resolved. This ensured for the stay of all those Serb who wished to stay in the territory of Western Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that topic in a minute. Let me just first focus you on this specific question: Following up on your answer, was this a discussion to permanently prevent Serbs from ever returning to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And I have plenty of evidence that I can present to this Chamber to corroborate my assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me pose -- show you two other exhibits and then I will give you a chance to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D690, please, at page 4 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a speech from the UN High Commissioner for Refugee, Mrs. Sagato Ogata on the 10th of October, and I want to ask you as someone who you have testified was personally responsible on the issue of refugee returns to Croatia and within Croatia, and I believe you have already testified as well that you worked with Mrs. Ogata, your understanding in the fall of 1995 whether the principles laid out by Mrs. Ogata in this speech were in fact the principles that the Republic of Croatia was adhering to, in terms of the policy concerning refugee returns. And in the second paragraph on your screen it says: "In order to carry out the return operation, I must emphasise the importance of having internationally recognised humanitarian principles. First of all, it must be voluntary. People must not be used as pawns." The next paragraph says: "Secondly, repatriation must take place in an organised phased manner." And then toward the bottom of that paragraph she says: "Returning large numbers of refugees to areas which are not yet ready to receive them can have very serious consequences not only for the refugees themselves but for the stability in the area concerned. I am thinking particularly of the still-fragile situation in the area of the Federation. "I envisage the repatriation process broadly taking place in three phases. The first should be the return of displaced persons within Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. During this initial post-settlement period, there are also likely to be further population movements as a result of the territorial adjustments between the parties." Then a few sentences down: "The second phase would involve repatriation from other Republics within the former Yugoslavia, and the third, return from countries which have granted temporary protection or resettlement." Now Mr. Granic, let me give you an opportunity here -- I know you want to speak about the issue of refugee returns.
