Did Croatia in fact then have a policy that internal returns were going to take place first and only later, as Mrs. Ogata says, when the security situation is sufficient, would there be returns from other Republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the principles stated by Mrs. Sagato Ogata, who was the High Commissioner for Refugees, were something that we strictly abided by. Finally, it was the way the refugee programme was put together in co-operation with them. The issue of displaced persons was being resolved within Croatia itself, and many of the Serbs could return once the Erdut agreement was signed and the peaceful reintegration process was on the move. During one of my visits to Belgrade, I agreed on several important matters with Minister Milutinovic. Firstly, we agreed that all refugees should be allowed to return; and, secondly, that private property is alienable. The same year, after the so-called Athens Declaration, that is to say, the talks held between heads of states and prime ministers there, a -- an agreement on the normalisation of relations between the FRY and Croatia was signed on the 23rd of August. It was Minister Milutinovic and I who signed the agreement. It was the first time that Serbia recognised Croatia within its territorial boundaries. The second issue was that all refugees could return and that private property was something that a person enjoys an alienable right to. After everything that was done thus far and following the principles laid down by Ms. Ogata in early April, together with the international community, meaning the UNHCR and the ICRC, as well as with the US and representatives of the EU, we began drafting the refugee programme which subsequently was adopted by the Croatian parliament and government later on in May and June that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, just so that the record is clear, all of these things that you've mentioned all took place after the conclusion of hostilities in November 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The process truly took off after the signing of the Erdut Agreement, and after that period, we began negotiating, talking with the FRY, and only after all those stages was the plan and programme finally finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday about a hypothetical example where an entire family from the so-called Krajina was -- let's say, in Serbia and had no family remaining in Croatia for humanitarian reunion. The fact that entire families that did not have a -- a family member in Croatia had to wait to return, was that consistent in your understanding with the policies laid out by UNHCR and Mrs. Ogata?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was fully consistent with the principles which were the same for Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the rest of the world. Those are the principles of the UNHCR applied to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in this instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about the importance of normalisation of relations with Yugoslavia in the context of refugee returns. And I'd like to show you a video-clip. This is a statement from -- a press release from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs being read out on the 28th of August 1995 after your meeting with the European Union Trojka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 1D3008. The transcript has been provided to the booths, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: The deputy prime minister and ministry of foreign affairs Dr. Mate Granic received today the representatives of the EU, the French ambassador to Zagreb, Jean Jacques Gaillard and first secretaries of the Spanish and Italian embassies, Camilo Villarino Marzo and Benedetto Laterri, at their own request, and also present at the meeting was the representative of the European Commission with the European Union Monitoring Mission ... "Press release from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: The representatives of the countries of the European Trojka expressed the EU's concern to Minister Granic regarding the situation involving human rights in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, emphasising that Croatia strongly condemns all incidents in those areas. Minister Granic said that these were individual incidents which before all show the level of frustration people have, and expressed his belief that with the stabilisation of civilian authorities the reasons for concern over the situation regarding human rights will no longer exist. With respect to the return of refugee Serbs from the liberated areas, Minister Granic pointed out that their return will unavoidably depend on the possibilities of achieving a final peaceful solution of the crisis in these areas and the normalisation of relations with the FRY. In present circumstances, individual requests will be received and processed in accordance with Croatian laws. Minister Granic confirmed that the Republic of Croatia will stay firm and consistent in the implementation of the policy of full respect of human and minority rights and that in this respect it will continue to pursue the path of its democratic and European orientation. Granic informed the representatives of the Europe Trojka that the possibility is also being considered to postpone the implementation of the provisions of constitutional law regarding the establishment of the Knin and Glina districts for a certain period of time until the situation in the field is fully assessed and stabilised. Granic additionally assured the European Trojka that such a possibly solution will in no manner have a negative impact on the constitutional guarantees and protection of minority rights."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, can you explain in a little bit more detail you mentioned there on the 28th of August that the issue of return was connected to the normalisation of relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were related issues because, at that time, as I have told earlier this morning, parts of the FRY army were still in Croatian territory. As late as the 28th of August, there was a threat of military intervention against Croatia by the FRY. On that day, there was still a danger of terrorist attacks in Croatia. In order to have the peaceful reintegration implemented, it was important for the FRY to accept that concept, and it was necessary for the FRY to recognise Croatia as a sovereign state. We were only recognised by the FRY on the 23rd of August, 1996. That was the reason why I put it that way at the time. I could only say that under the international conventions and humanitarian law we would only be able to deal with individual returns and only later that an organised plan be put in place. This was already discussed in Dayton and continued during our talks in August 1996. The overall process was concluded on the 23rd of August 1996 when the agreement on the normalisation of relations was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Granic, in that clip --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D3008 be marked, and I tendered it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit number D1821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1821 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, in that press statement, you also say that some of the incidents are the result of -- that before all show the level of frustration people have. And I'd like to show you one document, which is a press -- press article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 1D3006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I just want to give you an opportunity to comment on this. This is an article about an UN film showing slain civilians in Grubori, and the first part of the article deals extensively with video footage that had been broadcast about slain civilians in the village of Grubori and towards the middle then it says: "Almost every structure in this hill-side village was in flames, Knin said. Following a meeting with European union diplomats on Monday, Croatian foreign minister, Mate Granic, called the incidents isolated events which 'expressed the frustrations of people whose property was entirely destroyed'." Mr. Granic, I just want to clarify, your comment, was that related specifically to Grubori, or were you commenting generally on the situation in the liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have only Grubori in mind. It was a general remark. There was a lot of frustration and acts of revenge undertaken by different people. In cases where an earlier -- a Croatian village had been razed earlier, what followed was that a Serb village would be constantly be destroyed. That is what I had in mind, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, let me show you Exhibit D412, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can I suggest that this exhibit be tendered? I can use it in cross-examination. Grubori will be a topic. It might just be easier at this time for transparency purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a number should be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Granic, if you would allow me, you said it was a general comment. But did you intend to include the Grubori event in that comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only tell you that, at that point in time, as the foreign minister, I had heard of Grubori as an incident in which there were no crimes involved, based on the initial information we received. It pointed to the fact that this was a conflict incident, in which -- although I don't seem to be able to recall it clearly. In any case, the original information was not that there were crimes against civilians that had been committed but that this was a conflict with either the Croatian Army or the police. This is how it was presented in the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you intended at the time to include Grubori as one of the incidents you commented on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D412, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Minister Granic, this is a -- this is the normalisation of relations agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dated -- actually, it was sent on the 12th of September, 1996 to the United Nations but it's dated the 23rd of August of 1996. And I'm interested in page 3 of this document, at Article 7. Now Article 7(1) of the agreement ensured conditions for the free and safe return of refugees and displaced persons. Subsection (3) of Article 7 says: "The Contracting Parties shall declare a general amnesty for all acts committed in connection with the armed conflicts, except for the gravest violations of humanitarian law having the nature of war crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please. Subsection 5 says: "Each Contracting Party shall guarantee the same legal protection to the property of physical and legal persons having the citizenship of the other party, that is, being seated in the territory of the other party, as the one enjoyed by its own citizens, that is, its legal persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My first question, Mr. Granic, is the issue of general amnesty. Can you explain to us why a general amnesty was agreed for all acts committed in connection with the armed conflicts except for the gravest violations of humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General amnesty was agreed and signed, because without that precondition, it would have been impossible to make a plan for the return the refugees. On the other hand, without a general amnesty, there were no prerequisites for achieving a lasting peace and security for refugees. In the course of the process of peaceful reintegration, and this was separately agreed for individual areas of Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja, and uniformly agreed through this agreement for the entire territory of Croatia, including Croats who had run to the -- who had been -- who had run away from the Republic of Croatia into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there was an exception made in that provision for: "...violations -- for the gravest violations of humanitarian law having the nature of war crimes." Can you explain to the Chamber what transpired with respect to that provision as it relates to prosecuting Croatian Serbs for war crimes under that allowance, pursuant to this provision?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that this provision was in conformity with international treaties. The best international lawyers helped write it into our agreement. During the process of peaceful reintegration in the Croatian Podunavlje, General Klein, an American General and diplomat, who was a fantastic leader of the mission and who contributed to greatly to the success of that mission - it must have been one of the most successful missions of the UN ever - not only asked for general amnesty, he also asked for the number of accused of grave crimes be reduced first to 150, then to 85, and then to 25. That was not simple to do because it involved some pressure on the prosecutor's office. But even that was accepted for the sake of peaceful reintegration. That is a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, just so that the transcript is clear, you're talking about the reduction or a list of -- a maximum of 25 Croatian Serbs who could be prosecuted for the gravest violations of international humanitarian law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in light of what had transpired between 1991 and 1995 in the occupied territories and the number of persons who could be prosecuted being reduced to 25 for those events, as someone who was a vice-prime minister, do you -- was there any consequence, in terms of the prosecution of Croats for war crimes as a result of what was transpiring with the reduction of the number of Serbs who could be prosecuted to 25?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have so say this figure of 25 related to Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. Certainly this had an impact on the Croatian justice system, but not because of political pressures from the authorities. It had an impact because prosecutions of crimes by the Croatian side were also slowed down. All the crimes committed after Operation Storm were followed by prosecutions of 3.000 people for 4.000 crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And as part of this agreement on normalisation of relations at Article 7 subpart (5) there is this provision concerning property of -- people who are citizens of the other side - in this case, people who were living in or citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - enjoying the same rights to property as a citizen of the Republic of Croatia. Was that related to issue of refugee returns and preservation of property of Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was certainly related. This was a key paragraph which guaranteed the property of all refugees who still did not have Croatian citizenship. This agreement guaranteed their property regardless of whether they were going to apply for Croatian citizenship or not, or whether they were going to return or not. That's what this document guaranteed. The guarantees given to property by this -- by this agreement were indeed, very important, and this is one of the key paragraphs of the whole document. If I can only add one thing. Every refugee was given guarantees for their private property and legal property by this document. This applied to physical and legal persons alike, regardless of whether they were going to return or whether they're going to apply for Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would like to seek some clarification of the previous answer of the witness. Mr. Granic, you explained to us that a number of Serbs, from what I understand, accused of committing very serious crimes, in relation to Eastern Slavonia was reduced to 25 only. Then you went on to say that this had an impact on the system. And you then said because prosecutions of crimes by the Croatian side were also slowed down. Well, I understand that. And you said: "All the crimes committed after Operation Storm were followed by prosecution of 3.000 people for 4.000 crimes." We started with the prosecution of Serbs for very serious crimes, and you told us that they were reduced to 25, as far as Eastern Slavonia is concerned. Then you moved on to tell us how many Croats were prosecuted for crimes after Operation Storm. Now, could you tell us how many Serbs were prosecuted for serious crimes apart from the 25 in Eastern Slavonia, how many Serbs were prosecuted for, well, let's say, war crimes in addition to the 25 in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximation of -- approximately was it also in the numbers of 25 or 50, or was it by the hundreds, or was it by the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since most of them had run away, most of these were trials in absentia and these later provisions gave them the possibility of asking for a retrial. In other words, there were very few trials of such crimes, because there was no one to try. There were very few cases. I don't know the exact figure, but there were few. They were simply gone. Run away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said these were trials in absentia then. Could you give us an indication on how many trials in absentia were then held approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the number. I was the foreign minister. My job was foreign affairs and diplomacy. And I simply do not speculate on the number. There will be experts who can tell you that figure. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you could tell us that there were few, so you must have -- if you can say that there were few, you must have an idea, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for sure that there were 15 or 20 trials in absentia, but I cannot tell you the number, the exact number. I don't know it. It was not my field of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So numbers at a level approximately the same as the 25 you mentioned. Is that -- so by the tens and not by the hundreds. Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that that is roughly correct. Because all those who had committed the gravest crimes and who had command responsibility for crimes were then refugees or fugitives. There were very few persons to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but since that was not my area of work, I can't give you any figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're shifting from my question away. If you say there were only few to try, the others were fugitives, then you implicitly exclude the trials in absentia, and my question was focussing among other matters on -- and would at least include trials in absentia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I heard, Your Honours, I know certainly of 20 cases of trials in absentia. I don't know any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, including -- trials in absentia were at a level of approximately the same as the 25 you mentioned earlier, not in the tens, not in the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the number of people who were indicted and who were outside the territory of Slavonia and Baranja was much higher, in the hundreds, but the trials were never organised because they could not be reached. They could not be found. Only a few trials were held in absentia. But the number of indictees was in the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say trials which were concluded, that is, judgement rendered and sanction imposed, was by the tens. And that, in the hundreds, peoples were -- people were indicted, but those cases never came to a conclusion in terms of a judgement and sanctions imposed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit P2616, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a -- these are notes from a meeting -- or minutes of a meeting of the 33rd Session of the Council for Co-operation of the International Criminal Tribunal from 6 November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of this document, please, in English, and page 3 in the Croatian version. If we could -- it is actually at the bottom. Yes. At the bottom in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Ramljak who was the ministry of justice at the time and the parties have stipulated that he was the -- became the minister of justice in May of 1998. At point 2, he says: "Events that occurred after the Oluja operation. It seems that it is necessary to reassess the strategy taken two to three years ago, related to not processing the events and crimes committed in the aftermath of the operation, but we need to keep in mind that the council for co-operation with" -- it should be ICTY -- "is not obliged to discuss this issue." Now, Mr. Granic, you were present at this meeting. Can you help us understand what Mr. Ramljak was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admit this is not a very precise conclusion, but let me explain what actually happened at that meeting and a number of other meetings. At that time, there were discussions within our leadership, and we had differences, about whether the Tribunal in The Hague had jurisdiction over Operation Storm. My personal view was that the Tribunal had jurisdiction, and as you can see from these deliberations, a similar conclusion was ultimately adopted, and then the Tribunal or -- or whatever body was established by the Security Council would decide if it had jurisdiction or not. Within that body it was decided to address the Appeals Chamber of the ICTY, a request to decide whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction or not. It was a unified opinion, and we would have the support of the US in requesting from the Tribunal a formal opinion as to whether it was competent, whether it had jurisdiction over the Operation Storm. Another thing that was quite certain was that the councillor of the government of the Republic of Croatia, the advisor in fact, Mr. Rifkind suggested several options, all of them were unacceptable to us. One of them was to sue the Republic of Yugoslavia for genocide and that until that issue is resolved that Croatia should not co-operate with the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry to cut you off because I have limited amount of time left. My specific question is, did you know or do you know what Mr. Ramljak was referring to in saying that "... there was a strategy about not processing the events and crimes in the aftermath of the operation."

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vice-President Ramljak knew very well that by that time, around 3.000 individuals had been prosecuted, but he meant primarily co-operation with The Hague Tribunal and decisiveness in prosecuting the gravest cases, and he personally, like myself, was in favour of that. And when I say the gravest crimes, I mean committed both by Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, my question is in -- this strategy taken two to three years ago, specifically is he referring to the general amnesty that had been passed by the parliament two and a half years prior to that in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. General amnesty was adopted, the President granted clemency for some -- in some cases and all of this certainly had an impact on the justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, let me turn to the topic of Mr. Carl Bildt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you have dealt with this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I'm seeking some clarification. Mr. Granic, you said that the -- and let me -- that the policy of not processing events and crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm, that it was referring to the -- let me -- to the general amnesty that had been passed by parliament two and a half years prior to that, in 1996. I always understood, but please correct me when my understanding is wrong, that that amnesty was primarily aimed at not further prosecuting Serbs for crimes they had committed during the period of the RSK. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a correct understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the text we just read is that there was need for a reassessment, a strategy two to three years ago, related to not processing the events and crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm. The aftermath of Operation Storm, I don't understand to be the period, well, let's say, on from 6th or 7th of August, 1995. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know of any written document or any meeting where this was discussed or any strategy would have been adopted not to prosecute crimes. And I don't think there ever was a strategy in writing or a strategy agreed at state level. I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Granic, in one of the previous questions put to you by Mr. Misetic, you explained what was meant here by this. Now, I asked you simply, a simple question, the aftermath of Operation Storm, what period in time that would cover, and you start explaining that you are not aware of any policy, apparently a policy on which you gave your opinion in the previous question from Mr. Misetic. My question, apart from that was quite simple: Aftermath of Operation Storm, what do you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand this as follows: In fact, I suppose that Vice-President Ramljak meant the time when the general amnesty decision was made. He meant that period. Not just after Operation Storm. At least I don't think so, if I understood your meaning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking you, as a matter of fact, but you now tell me that what Mr. Ramljak concluded when he said the aftermath of Operation Storm, that he was talking about the period in time around the amnesty laws, when the amnesty laws were adopted. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's probably what he meant. As for the situation after Operation Storm, you can see from deliberations at government sessions, we advocated very vociferously the prosecution of all crimes including crimes committed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I asked you earlier whether the main purpose of the amnesty laws were to cover crimes committed by Serbs during the RSK period, and you confirmed that. And now I do understand from your last answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you confirm it again. Now from your last answer, I take it that the -- the strategy related to not processing the events and crimes committed doesn't refer -- does refer to the period after Operation Storm, that is, after the RSK period. I'm not slightly but totally confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to put further questions to the witness it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, let's try to clarify this. The Law on General amnesty applied not just to Serbs, it applied to everything that took place between 1990 and August 1996, correct? Committed by anyone in connection with the armed conflict except for serious violations of international humanitarian law, correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Under the law crimes committed after Operation Storm, not classified as war crimes and connected to the armed conflict would have fallen under the general amnesty act passed in September 1996. Was that your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ramljak who was not in the Croatian government until May of 1998, I'm asking you, was it your understanding that he is referring to the fact that many crimes were prosecuted but other crimes -- many crimes were not because they would have fallen under the provisions of the General Amnesty Act passed in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, Mr. Ramljak was the vice-president of the democratic union government. What he meant here in item 2, I'm not sure, because such a strategy had never been adopted. The only thing I can say is that it's quite certain that, at the moment the general amnesty was adopted, with clear definition of the period to which it applied, as Mr. Misetic said, it was quite certain at that time when the number of local Serbs who were indicted was reduced from several hundred to 25, it had an impact on the justice system, although I'm quite sure that no one in our political leadership had ever given any instructions about that. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let me just clarify part of your answers to the Presiding Judge. The Chamber has received in evidence many, many documents from the Security Council and the President of the Security Council throughout 1996 up to the passage of the general amnesty law insisting on the passage of a general amnesty law for -- because it related to the issue of peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia and the return of Serbs. So the law was passed under pressure concerning the issue of Serb returns but it was -- it broadly covered all acts that fall within the provision of the law between 1990 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's precisely how it was. It covered all acts, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All acts except violations of international law?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put things very clear to you, Mr. Granic. In this document, it is mentioned that there had been a strategy related to not processing the events and crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm. Now, this Chamber, the evidence this Chamber has received is not that a substantial number of crimes were committed after Operation Storm by Serbs. Do you have any information that a substantial number of crimes were committed by Serbs in the Krajina territory in the aftermath of Operation Storm, which I consider to be -- well, let's say, on from the 6th or 7th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beyond any dispute, a great number of crimes in that area was not committed by Serbs after Operation Storm. Simply because there were relatively few of them who had remained; and those who remained were mostly elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would we therefore agree that if there ever had been a strategy of not processing events and crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm, that that would not primarily have focused on crimes committed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hypothetically we could say that, if such a strategy had ever existed. As the foreign minister and deputy prime minister, I'm not aware of any strategy not to prosecute. We can only discuss whether there was full decisiveness of the justice system to prosecute all crimes. That is something we could discuss. I personally was in favour of greater firmness in prosecutions, of crimes committed by Croats. But as for any signed or agreed strategy not to prosecute, that certainly did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The terminology is processing the crimes. But apart from this semantic issue, thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic. I'm looking at the clock at the same time, and I notice that this is already beyond the time we usually take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I had just one last question for him on one topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then -- please put that question to Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have Exhibit D747, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, the Chamber has heard and seen several times Carl Bildt's statements on the 4th of August, his statements in Geneva on 6th of August, the Chamber has seen the memo concerning your meting with Mr. Bildt on 6th of August, concerning allegations of the shelling of Knin, et cetera. This is a letter written to you -- by you to the president of the European Commission. I believe it is dated 8 -- 8 August. And essentially the Republic of Croatia is declaring Mr. Bildt persona non grata and you are complaining about Mr. Bildt's allegations, et cetera. Can tell us why the Republic of Croatia declared him persona non grata and what impact that had in terms of your relationship with Mr. Bildt throughout the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, that is to say, the first day of Operation Storm, Mr. Bildt accused Croatia of having barbarically shelled Knin, especially civilians. On the very first day of the operation, it was a very grave accusations for which we knew was unfounded. There was no barbaric shelling of civilians, it was not random, and it was not excessive. All of the information I had from several sources including some Croatian Generals, the Generals who were in charge of the operation, all that went completely contrary to that allegation. The information was that the Croatian Army behaved fully professionally on that day and that the accusation that came from Mr. Bildt was the worse thing that Croatia had to face on day one. That is why I reacted so brusquely. I spoke to Mr. Bildt in Geneva on the 6th, and I say -- I'll try to quote my words at that time, But there was no excessive or random shelling and that there were no significant casualties among civilians. I personally visited Knin on the 8th to reassure myself of that. With the assistance of Mr. Holbrooke, we managed to patch up our mutual relationship in Dayton but everything I said on that day came as a result of being deeply hurt both as a person and as the minister because it completely went against everything that took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. I do understand, Mr. Kay, you have given up your time which means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it seemed that the matters that were being dealt with by Mr. Misetic, as I told the Court, there would be a convergence of interest. If I could just mention one thing. There were three documents produced by Mr. Misetic: D1813, D1814, and D1815 which had passages within them that would I have brought to the Court's attention through this witness. They weren't statements by this witness at government meetings, but by others that were there, and it would have to been to hopefully assist the Court in looking at those matters. It seems to me that this is a forensic exercise that could be dealt with in a completely different way by me just telling the Court that from our position we consider those to have been very important exhibits and asking the Court, as we know it will, to look at those documents with -- with care, because they contain important statements at the time. I think that that saves court time rather than uses the exercise of questioning to bring something to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which more or less would create a situation in which Mr. Misetic tendered documents into evidence, and that you deal with the same documents more or less on a bar table basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, you explain why concern portions of those documents deserve specific attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that either in an oral submission or a written submission you tell us which specific portions you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue to hear the evidence of the witness, I'd like to briefly address the matter of expert Witness MM-23. A report is there, a lot of the material on which the expert has formed his opinion is not available in English, from what I understand. That, at least, was what the Prosecution told us on the 9th of November. And the Chamber wonders whether that situation is still the same, because to adopt views of an expert, if have you no access to the material on which he has -- on the basis of which he has formed his opinions might be not a very transparent exercise. It might be a great problem for the Chamber even to assess the solidity of these opinions. Could the chamber hear from the Markac Defence any further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Honour, I will let Mr. Mikulicic address the substantive issues but you will see our response to the Prosecution's motion is due month, so we will have a response to the Chamber by then. But as far as a direct answer to your question, Your Honour, I will let Mr. Mikulicic address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is correct that a portion of the material referred to by the expert witness was not translated; however, all of the material they referred to was handed over for translation. We receive it in successive portions, and as we receive them we disclose them to the Prosecutor. In addition to that, through our contacts with the Prosecution and based on their choice of priorities, we forward material for translation. Also given some specific sources that the expert witness referred to, we indicated to the Prosecutor that these are public sources, such as books, and we also provided Internet links and libraries where such publications could be per used. We are doing our utmost to enable the Prosecutor as much access to the material as possible. Of course, we are not completely happy with the process as well. But as you know from your own experience, Your Honour, that the problem of translation is something that occurs in all cases and that in a way it also effects both parties and the documents they submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. The Chamber just wants to clearly indicate that not having access to underlying sources that that may create a problem in the -- in the use of the expert report as evidentiary material and that's, therefore, to perhaps emphasise the importance of having the material available. Mr. Mikulicic, whether the evidence is to be found in public sources, if I can't read it, I can't read it publicly or privately, it doesn't make that much of a difference. But I do understand that it has your full attention and the Chamber wanted to ensure that this has the proper attention. I only address this matter. I didn't -- we are still waiting for a response by the Markac Defence on other matters which were raised by the Prosecution but this one was a relatively neutral but also a relatively important one. So, therefore, we addressed it. Then -- Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Granic. You have written a book with the title: Foreign Affairs Behind the Screens of Politics. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have 65 ter 7484 on the screen, and I have prepared excerpts from the book. It's 14 pages in English, and 15 in B/C/S. The whole book is about 230 or 240 pages. And throughout my cross-examination, I will be referring to parts of -- of the excerpt and perhaps it could receive now an exhibit number, MFI and later, if foundation is laid, I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from your use of this document, I take it that if there are any other relevant portions that a selection of the portions could be expanded in consultation with the Defence teams. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as P2662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it keeps that status for a while. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony yesterday you have discussed the speech of President Tudjman at the UN General Assembly in 1994. This is D1799 but we don't need to -- to get it. And there he talks about the focus on protection for human rights. That's a quote from -- from that speech. Do you remember that -- that -- having discussed that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you know him, Dr. Granic, you know President Tudjman. And I think it's your assessment, and I quote from your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is on page 3 in English and B/C/S that: "He was a politician of the old style and didn't understand respect for human rights."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you talk about an instance in Bosnia which you have discussed in your direct evidence as well. You remember, I think you have called Mr. Boban about the closure of the camps. So let me quickly read what you -- what you say here about this topic. And on Wednesday, you discussed that at page 24622. I quote now from -- from your book: "When I informed him about the existence of the Croat-held camps for the prisoners of war, Bosniak civilians in BiH, he became infuriated and changed the expression of his face, comprehending that this is strongly damaging Croatia. However, he was a politician of the old style, who did not understand the issue of respecting the human rights. He thought that the solution of that problem was a mechanism for exerting pressure on Croatia. When I would mention it, he would immediately respond with a counterquestion. What are [sic] the Americans doing in Vietnam, the French in Algeria, and the British in the colonies? In his opinion, those were the imperative consequences of war. That was also the reason why he did not steadily insist on the investigations when that was necessary, but he never prevented them. That is why I think that nobody can refer to Tudjman, regardless of the duty one was performing. Everyone, that committed, ordered, or failed to prevent crimes has one's own responsibility." Do you stand by what you wrote in your book?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I firmly stand by every word I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So his comments about human protection for human rights before the General Assembly was for public consumption, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the official position of the Republic of Croatia, which had been discussed with the innermost political circles. To be more precise, the closest of his associates - that is to say, we - prepared that speech and he stood by it. He was a statesman and a historian. He was not a diplomat. And as I said, he was of the old school regarding human rights. It is true that he mainly believed it to be as a pressure mechanism employed by the west and exercised on Croatia. Frequently even small, minor incidents were used to exert pressure on Croatia. However, Tudjman was the person who supported me in all of the most important moves to stop the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to close down camps, and without his support, I would not have been able to do anything. Therefore, at the end of the sentence, at the end of the paragraph, I stated that each one of us has his or her own responsibilities and duties. In all main activities I undertook, diplomatic activities in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, I enjoyed President Tudjman's support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. Let's move to a second short topic, the Geneva negotiations. In your book, and this is at page 6 in English and 8 in B/C/S, you talk about the fact that you discussed the negotiations with President Tudjman. And then you say that "visibly content" -- it's about the 12th line in English: "Tudjman accepted my opinion and informed me that Thorvald Stoltenberg was insisting on the meeting between the rebel Serbs and representatives of the Croatia government in Geneva. It was clear to both of us that he anticipated that we were soon to launch a determined reintegration of our occupied areas. Tudjman decided that the Croatian delegation in Geneva will be led by his counsellor for internal affairs, Ivic Pasalic. He had precise instructions what to accept in Geneva and he strictly followed them. We did not expect any serious results from that meeting, but we had to get it over with before the decisive battle." So it was predetermined what would come out from the Geneva meetings. Is that a fair interpretation of your comment here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to put a full context in that question it will be suggested from our side to read the next, the following sentence. Exactly on the point where Mr. Waespi stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, although everyone is free to put the quote as he wishes to a witness, it sometimes is more efficient to not split up matters. If you could follow the suggestion of Mr. Mikulicic that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Those days our intelligence officers intensively intercepted Milosevic's telephone conversations so we positively knew that Belgrade was not ready for a serious military retaliation to the Croatian military and police operation. We had many strategic advantages."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything I wrote is fully accurate. This means the following: Mr. Pasalic had instructions to accept only an arrangement on peaceful reintegration, and that is something he could do immediately. We did not want any postponements. Absolutely no postponements. Why? Because we were being dragged throughout the mud for four years. They never sincerely approached any peaceful reintegration negotiations. Throughout that period they were committing ethnic cleansing in the territory they controlled. We did not want to miss out on this opportunity, because we had the most favourable international circumstances. We did not want to miss this opportunity to help and save Bihac, which is something I have discussed extensively. Therefore, Mr. Pasic was under instructions to either immediately accept peaceful reintegration or to refuse the proposal. This is exactly the way things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to a slightly different aspect now. The warnings from the international community before launching Operation Storm. There were warnings, were there not, for instance, from the German government that they would not support such military actions and that it would not be able to protect Croatia from a possible diplomatic reaction in this case. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fair assessment would be that Germany said that publicly they could not support us. I think President Kohl sent a letter to President Tudjman. However, one needs to mention that, at that time the European Union did not play a decisive role in the stopping of the war in establishing of peace. It was the US policy that did that. European political world with Owen-Stoltenberg and the rejection of the plan in late 1993 handed over initiative to US policy makers. In our assessments, we relied exclusively on the extent by which our operation went hand in hand with the American peace initiative, and we were 100 per cent right on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we quickly could go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Yes, it is only now that the French translation has finished. Mr. Granic, even if you would like to leave before the weekend, it certainly will not help to speak any quicker, because this sometimes has a counter-productive effect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your -- for this caution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could turn into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to 65 ter 7476 which is an interview you gave with Slobodna Dalmacija on the 31st of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember, after so many years, having given that interview?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember having given the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on page 4 in English and page 1 in B/C/S; and in B/C/S, in Croatian, it's the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think that's the right one. I want -- if we go back to 7477. I'm sorry. 65 ter 7477. Yes, that's the interview I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In Croatian, Dr. Granic, it's the second column from the right; and in English, it's page 4. There it is stated, answering a question about decision and support what happened immediately prior to Operation Storm, you say that: "A day before Operation Storm, at the meeting of the VONS President Tudjman read the messages from Clinton, Yeltsin, Kohl, Chirac Major, all of them advised Croatia not to go into a military operation." And then you go on to say that: "...the decision to launch the operation was naturally the President's, since VONS was only an advisory body but they were fully supportive of such a decision." Do you stand by what you told the journalist of Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do. I stand by everything that's been said here. But in journalistic term it is not so clear and requires additional explanation. No one at that time said, no, you can't go ahead with this operation, like President Clinton said on the 12th and the 13th November 1994 concerning the creation of the corridor towards Bihac, or when State Secretary Christopher called me on the 14th October 1995 saying, Stop there, don't go to Banja Luka. State Secretary Christopher called me and Mr. Holbrooke called Tudjman. In this case, there were only mild recommendations to refrain. There was no clear message, Stop, do not go. My point in this interview was to make clear that it was not an agreement or an understanding wherein the US said, No, don't do that. In this case, President Tudjman made the decision himself, after evaluating all the international circumstances, as extremely favourable, and it was our judgement that we were complementing the American state initiative very well. Indeed, we had given prior notification to the US, and that was my point in this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2663.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2663 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talked a lot about Bihac in your evidence in-chief and also a moment ago. But it's correct to say, Dr. Granic, that Bihac was just one factor in the decision to go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Prosecutor. It was one of the factors, but it was a very important one. Ever since November 1994, Bihac had been a constant topic in our talks with the Bosniak side, and a subject of their requests for assistance. It was just one of the factors, but a very important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But were you aware that President Tudjman, on 31st of July, 1995, and this is the famous Brioni meeting at which you did not attend, I take it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not attend. But during the break, President Tudjman called me on the phone and asked my opinion in case he decided to go forward with the police and military Operation Storm. He wanted me to give an evaluation from a diplomatic and international legal point of view but especially diplomatic evaluation of possible reactions by allies, friendly states, and reactions of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you tell -- you, when he talked to you, or did you become aware otherwise that President Tudjman during that meeting said the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is P461, English page 1, B/C/S page 2. I will read the relevant parts: "Therefore, it is my opinion that our main objective can no longer be to break through to Bihac." And then the next quote: "But if" -- and it's just the next paragraph -- "but if in the forthcoming days we are to undertake further operations then Bihac can only serve as some sort of pretext and something of a secondary nature." And there is another quote on page 10 in English and page 20 in B/C/S. Page 10 it starts at the bottom, and I quote: "President Tudjman says: Generals, officers, although we must not do anything in an ill-conceived manner, we must proceed from the fact that we have achieved such successes from West Slavonia and now in Bosnia, that we gained the trust of the people, and that we have the goodwill of the army, the support of a good part of international public opinion, while the enemy is utterly demoralised." And then the final sentence in this paragraph: "Nevertheless, I think that the political situation is so favourable that we should focus on entering Knin as soon as possible." That's the Supreme Commander speaking that Bihac is a -- some sort of pretext. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting, but I know very well what the positions of President Tudjman were. I know it because I talked to him during those days, including that day. The main objective was to reach Croatian borders and free the occupied territories of Croatia. The second goal was Bihac. Those were the two most important objectives. Why Bihac? In your quotation, the President does not speak of Bosnia and Herzegovina; whereas our third most important goal was to end the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and help our allies. The president, as the Supreme Commander, was telling the soldiers what our objective was, and that was to reach the borders. Therefore, I was not at that meeting, I cannot give you an interpretation, but I know to a certainty what the position was. And I believe you will see precisely from any US documents what I said to Peter Galbraith, what we discussed with the Americans. The first goal was to reach the Croatian borders and, of course, in -- for this objective Knin, as a centre of intelligency was an important target. That's why the action was led by one of the best if not the best Croatia General. The second goal was Bihac, and the third goal was to help Bosnia and Herzegovina and the US peace initiative. But in the order of priorities, the first one was to reach the borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm looking at the clock. We have to finish for this morning. We will resume at 3.30 this afternoon in this same courtroom. We adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon in this extended session for today. Judge Kinis is, for urgent personal reasons, unable to continue sitting in this case for a short period, that means this afternoon. And Judge Gwaunza and myself concluded that it's in the interest of justice to continue to hear the case. And, therefore, we ordered that we would continue. The reason that Judge Gwaunza is moving from one side to the other is just a matter of logging in at the right computer. So just for those who wondered what happened, this is what happened. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, usually if we have only a break during the day I do not remind the witness that he is still bound by the solemn declaration so I will refrain from doing that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before the break, Dr. Granic, you said that the Operation Storm, I think, was led by one of the best, if not the best Croatian General. Whom did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ante Gotovina. Of course, the special police force led by General Markac was also involved. The force enjoyed the highest level of reputation in Croatia since the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which force do you mean? Which force? All the units participating in Operation Storm or specific units?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "the special police force," I meant the special police force as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. You have been very close to President Tudjman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you accepted his leadership, and you almost saw a father-figure in him.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted his leadership. At that point in -- that was a historic moment for Croatia, I believed that it was important to have such a figure for a president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think Defence minister Susak, he was one of President Tudjman's closest associates. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I would say, that up until his death, he was the closest associate of President Tudjman's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did he die?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died in 1998, in early May. I think it was the 4th or the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we're talking about Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, likewise, General Gotovina belonged to the circle of Mr. Susak's closest associates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. General Gotovina was one of the closest associates of Minister Susak's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. You discuss all that in your book. Now, you stated in paragraph 8 of your witness statement, which is now Defence exhibit 1797, as follows: "As the minister of foreign affairs and the deputy prime minister, during and after military ... police Operation Storm ... the operation of liberation of the occupied areas of Croatia apart from other numerous international political activities, I participated in, I radically fought for obedience of Geneva Convention's international humanitarian law." Now, why do say that? Why did you have to "fight" for the Geneva Conventions or for the obedience of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, quite clearly, it was an operation of a greater scale and because such operations inevitably have consequences. There was nothing to point us to what might come after Operation Storm. However, I always made this issue quite clear, and I will be quite precise. When, on the 21st of July, sometime between 1200 and 1300 hours I spoke to President Tudjman, I said that the most significant and memorable thing that we will be remembered by all is how soon we will finish the operation and how strongly we will adhere to international law and international conventions. I said the same on the 3rd of August, 1995, when we had a meeting of the National Security Council. I said that our international friends are going to judge us by how closely we stick to the provisions of international and humanitarian law. It was my personal position, therefore. If I may make just one more point. Our friends worldwide, including the Americans and Germans, alerted us to this fact, especially the US and Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just if we could check the date on page 87, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my line numbering is a bit different. Is it -- it's not a July but the August reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My transcript actually is different than the LiveNote in the centre. In -- on yours it is page 86, line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your last answer, you said: "When" -- and then you gave a date, "sometime between 1200 and 1300 hours I spoke to President Tudjman." Which date were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 31st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This being corrected, please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the Germans -- or the Americans they were referring to the commission of war crimes prior to Operation Storm by the Croatian Army. That's why they told you to be careful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cautioned us about adherence to international conventions. We didn't spoke about -- speak about the details. We spoke strictly about the abidance by the provisions of laws and customs of war and international humanitarian law. In other words, treatment of refugees, or, rather, of potential refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you write in your statement you had to fight radically for it, did you have to fight with somebody, or was it generally accepted, your advice?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody contradicted me on that score. There was nobody who was opposed to that or who would publicly oppose the position I set out, and I myself did work in favour of that. Mr. Prosecutor, in 1991, I was on the wartime government, and before I became a member of the government as the dean of the faculty of medicine, I was on -- on the -- a member of the medical corps. And in 1991, we had already, at that time, issued instructions to soldiers on how to behave themselves and respect Geneva Conventions, should conflicts break out. So this was my position throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But these instructions didn't work at all times. War crimes were committed by Croatian forces, for instance in the Medak Pocket operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During operation Medak Pocket, crime did happen, and it is true that crime had been committed on the Croatian side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I'm talking primarily now about war crimes by the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were crimes committed by the Croatian Army too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you do remember having received a letter dated 1st of October by Mr. Mazowiecki, and that's 1993, about what was happening in Medak Pocket. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Prosecutor. I do remember that. And I will tell the Trial Chamber the extent of what I remember well. Operation Medak Pocket came to my notice on the morning when it started. In accordance with his constitutional powers, the President of the Republic at the proposals of Minister Jarnjak and General Bobetko, proposed that the operation be launched following a period during which Gospic had been constantly shelled, and there were civilian casualties as well as a massacre committed against policemen. The reason was the utter insecurity where -- and it was under these circumstances the population had to live. The operation was completed successfully. That was what I knew about it. When I received the letter from Mazowiecki, according to the procedure in place, I asked the information from the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, since I had a small human rights department, although, at the level of the government, there was a deputy prime minister, Professor Kostalic [phoen] who was actually in charge of that department, of the matter. My first answer or response to Mr. Mazowiecki was not a complete one. I became aware of it later on, however, I provided him with the information that I had at the time and that had been prepared for me. However, the information was not full. As soon as I had all the information in possession, including the fact that there was lack of discipline on the part of the Home Guard, that there were casualties among the civilians as well, and as soon as I received that information, it was at a later date, I believe it was actually at a VONS meeting, I took the following steps: I asked from the President of the Republic that an inquiry be launched immediately into this, and that the responsible individuals be punished. This was what I was able to do -- what was within my power to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic? For the completion of the record, I would like to called up 65 ter 7500 and ask you to confirm that this is this the letter Mr. Mazowiecki, at the time, Special Rapporteur, on the former Yugoslavia has written to you on 1st of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that this is the letter. I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can scroll down to the bottom, we see at the left hand your name. I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just get a proffer from Mr. Waespi as to the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: To the evidence in general or to this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The relevance of this letter and the Medak Pocket operation to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It shows that war crimes were committed in the past, that the Croatian Army, as we suggest, was prone to committing crimes and it wasn't taken seriously. That's the relevancy of this aspect. That's number one. Number two, the witness talked about Medak Pocket and other operations like Grahovo and Glamoc in his witness statement and he called it I think liberation operations, and I want to state the record clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I guess our position is that the Prosecution, I don't believe, put on evidence of the Medak Pocket operation in its case in chief so to the extent this is now being added for substantive value, I think it opens up new topics that heretofore have not been addressed in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi also told that the witness talked about a Medak Pocket operation in his examination-in-chief so, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't recall it off the top of my head. And I don't know the context of what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 20 of the witness statement, D1797. This is a reference to the military liberations operations of Grahovo and Glamoc, to which I will turn in a second. And I'm quite sure that the witness talked about Medak Pocket yesterday or the day before in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see it in paragraph 20 of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just mention that it relates to Grahovo and Glamoc only in this part. Medak Pocket is in paragraph 17. "I was active, and I participated in reaching decisions on the actions of the Croatian armed force with the purpose of liberation of the occupied territory for instance action Miljevacki Plateau whose objective was to disable the bombardment of Sibenik from that areas, Action Maslenica, action Medak Pocket, Flash, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm fairly sure that the evidence of Mr. Theunens addressed Medak Pocket as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the prejudice under 89(C) to the Defence, given that there's no direct relevance to any -- to my client, certainly, of the Medak Pocket operation to this case. It is two years prior to the indictment period. And it opens up, I think, areas that are not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, Mr. Misetic. Although the relevance is not very high, certainly the fact that it was two years before the Operation Storm is -- is certainly not a matter which would prevent Mr. Waespi from dealing with the matter. I think that we received quite a lot of evidence on what happened and still are about to receive further evidence about what happened of the years since 1991, even. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Waespi. Just to add on this topic which have to have in mind that the operation Medak Pocket was an issue of a separate trial proceedings which was conducted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Medak Pocket was a matter which was the subject of a case which was initially before this Tribunal and then later was referred to the local courts. The Chamber is aware of that. I take it that Mr. Waespi is aware of that. The ruling is there. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit number P2664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2664 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There's also a reference in Mr. Galbraith's diary at P458 that links Medak Pocket to comments made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, Mr. Waespi, as I said before, the ruling is there so there is no need to give further ammunition to a matter which has been decided already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And likewise, Dr. Granic, war crimes were committed in the operation for the liberation of Grahovo and Glamoc at the end of July 1995, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shouldn't very have specificity about this, war crimes where committed the previous questions about Medak Pocket, in my submission, were absolutely meaningless, and the witness is being asked to agree to something, war crimes were committed, well, what war crimes? A prisoner being slapped? What exactly? If anything is going to be done with this, it has to be put in a way that the witness can effectively deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the witness felt that he was in a position to confirm as far as Medak Pocket is concerned, but, Mr. Waespi it goes without staying that the probative value if there's no specificity whatsoever in relation to the war crimes, that it's not of great assistance for the Chamber to determine the matters before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Are you aware that crimes were committed during the operation liberation of Grahovo and Glamoc which you describe in paragraph 20 of your witness statement, crimes committed by the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the Grahovo-Glamoc operation was the result of an agreement reached with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was a key operation to assist in the lifting of the burden of Bihac. Secondly, from a military point of view, the operation was a successful one, and it helped a great deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Waespi did not invite you to tell us the whole story of this operation but asked a specific question, which was: Whether you were aware that crimes were committed during the operation liberation of Grahovo and Glamoc, which you describe in paragraph 20 of your witness statement. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at around about the time of the start of Operation Storm, say for the fact that the operation had been successful, I didn't know anything else. There were no additional discussions about it, and nobody told me anything about it. It was only many years later that I heard that that particular operation had been accompanied by destruction and certain other events. The details surrounding it are still not known to me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
