utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show the witness a document, 65 ter 1883.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an document dated 13 August 1995 signed by commander Captain Adinajic [phoen] from the 72nd Military Police Battalion. And it states in page 2, English and Croatian, that the last paragraph on the following day, and this is the 30th of July, 1995, as we can see from the previous text: "On the following day, members of the Croatian Army 4th Guards Brigade and the 7th Guards Brigade, as well as certain groups (Croatian Army 114th Brigade, 126th Home Guard Regiment) ... came into the broad area of Grahovo from surrounding area, began setting fire to houses in Grahovo and the surrounding villages, in an organised fashion." Now, I take it you weren't aware of this kind of information about what was happening just a few days before Operation Storm was launched and before you made your comments about respect for the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as this document is concerned, I didn't know about it. I have never seen it before. And as for the events like setting fire to things and destruction, as I said earlier on, I heard about all that much later, so I didn't know about this. Especially not during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. Susak, and there is evidence about this in this case, he didn't tell you that he passed by Glamoc and Grahovo on the 1st of July and was reported to be very disappointed by burning and looting which is especially noticeable in the 4th and 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's from P71, the Split Military District diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's nothing you were made aware of by Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it isn't. I didn't know about that. At that time, and I can tell you straightaway, we met each other at a meeting but we never discussed this, nor did I have any knowledge or awareness of any of this, coming from Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So your comment about radically observe Geneva Conventions, that came out of the blue or based on the experience in 1991, but not by recent events that might have triggered your comment. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Very specifically, over the past two day, I have been testifying here and responding to questions from Defence counsel about how the government conducted itself and how I behaved personally after Operation Storm when we received information about the setting fire to houses, looting, and individual crimes, which were committed. All I can say is that sometime in the period between the 25th of August, up until the 1st of September, for example, somewhere during that period of time, when I received information to the effect that the scope of those events and crimes exceeded what I thought they -- what I thought had been happening, when I received this information, then in the space of two days, I talked to all the most responsible people in the country. First of all, with the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak. I talked to him, and I confronted him with the information that I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we will come to that as it relates to Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- if that's what you are talking about. But let me just ask a final question on this topic. You were according to paragraph 17 of your witness statement, involved about reaching decisions in the liberation of Grahovo and Glamoc, but you're saying you don't really know what was happening, at least not when it comes to crimes. Is that a fair assessment of your -- description of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a very fair assessment, but I didn't know at that time what was happening in Glamoc and Grahovo except for the fact that there had been a successful military operation which vitally helped operation Storm, so that's the only information and knowledge I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. Let's go now to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just -- just so that the record is clear. Page 86, line 18, Mr. Waespi says he is quoting from paragraph 8 of the witness statement which is now Defence exhibit 1797, and Mr. Waespi uses the word "radically," and maybe I'm wrong but I can't see the word "radically" in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it is there at least in my translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not the translation in e-court that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe we can go to the B/C/S original. This is what I have. Dated 12th May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S original, the document I'm aware of is the document which was filed on the -- on the 11th of November, a filing -- no, corrigendum, 10th of November, filed the 11th of November, in which we find a corrected version of the statement. That's the one I have got in front of me. And I can easily look at the e-court version, if there's any reason to assume that it is not the same. And you were quoting from paragraph 8. I do not see the word "radically" appearing in paragraph 8, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But this was certainly the witness statement that was served on us at one point in time. I think there was an issue about the dates. We had two or three different dates. I apologise if I'm working from an outdated witness statement, but then I should have been told that the next statement, the new one is -- has changed or at least a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, on the 11th of November, a motion was filed, to which a corrigendum attached. Now, the motion, as such --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- doesn't say that much. It mainly says that earlier you had attached an incomplete version of the English translation and now you say we now attach the complete translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to solve this problem, Your Honour. Mr. Waespi is dealing with the official translation which we obtained recently and we, of course, transferred it to the OTP office. And it is quite obvious then in paragraph 8 there is no such word as "radically."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... What's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we are looking in the original of the statement then we could easily find that the word "radically" is really in that paragraph. So I don't know where the problem lies, but obviously Mr. Waespi is right when it seceded an original version of the -- Mr. Granic's statement where Mr. Granic is referring that he was radically fighting for the Geneva Convention in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, I would prefer that the B/C/S version is read so that we -- I know that -- I'm not asking the interpreters to give the final interpretation but just to find out whether there are any other matters which should be of concern to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could read this paragraph if -- for the purpose of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, this is not in order to get an authorised translation but just to see whether this, at first sight, seems to be the only problem or whether there may be more problems, especially since apparently a word is left out. And if you would allow me ... Please proceed. Mr. Mikulicic is reading paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in the original paragraph 8 is going like this. I will read it in Croatian. [Interpretation] "As minister of foreign affairs and deputy prime minister during and after the military police Operation Storm to liberate the occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia, except for numerous extra political activities, I radically strove for the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law to be respected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if the problem is limited to that one word. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender 65 ter 1883, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2665.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to come now to the crimes that were -- that occurred in the aftermath of Operation Storm. And you devote one entire chapter entitled: "Crimes" in your book, and this is now P2662. And I would like to call this document up. And it starts in English page 9, and in B/C/S, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And main issues are, you know, when did you hear about the crimes, what did you discuss with the people you mention in -- in this chapter. Let me just read you the relevant part. "I received first information about the crimes in the liberated areas from Peter Galbraith, and then other information came from other diplomates and journalists." I'm going stop here. If you recall, when did Peter Galbraith inform you about the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were talks between the 25th and 30th of August, 1995, although, up until that time, I had also received information from Peter Galbraith, so I received information before that too, but they were within the frameworks in general of information which I would receive, that is, official information that I would receive from the Ministry of the Interior. Now, the information that I write about in my book are pieces of information that I received after the 25th, when it was obvious to me that the scope and scale of the destruction, that is to say, setting fire to facilities, crime, looting, and so on, was greater than I had had information about before that. So, as I say, it's sometime between the 25th and 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were involved -- you were informed by Mr. Galbraith during that period?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith and some journalists, the Helsinki board and so on so I received information from at least three sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you tasked people in the ministry, verifying that, that occurs in that period, between the 25th and the 30th of August?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. When I received that, then, first of all, I had the information checked out. I verified it. And the information that they received, that is to say, the people who were in charge of this with me, confirmed that the scope of crimes was greater than I knew about. Until my letter to Kinkel, for example, and Lasso-Ayala and so on. And that the scale of the crimes was greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who told you about the scale, and what information triggered your assessment that it's now really becoming a problem? Do you remember what piece of information or what conversation you had made you really change your opinion that it's no longer just media propaganda, as you said, but it is now something that you have got to address?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply within the space of two or three days I received more and more information coming in, which I checked out, and the information proved to be correct. And to be more precise, at that point in time, from the Ministry of Interior, my people responsible in the ministry confirmed this, that yes, the scale was greater. So when I was certain about that, then I went into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the information received was from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They confirmed the information that I had received myself. Minister Jarnjak confirmed this information, because I went to him to consult him first because, of course, he was minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, this meeting with Minister Jarnjak, which is referred to at the bottom of page 9 in English, that happened -- can you be precise of when it happened in that time-frame again, towards August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph in English on page 2 -- page 10, you write: "Immediately after the meeting with Jarnjak, I met with Valentic. ... a brief conversation -- in a brief conversation I learned that he was also partially informed about those developments. He was angry and fully supported me when I said I was going meet with Tudjman and ask him to prevent murders, robberies, and arsons." So, again, that meeting with Mr. Valentic happened towards the end of August?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. Valentic was the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. And he strongly condemned such things and lent full support, or, rather, ask that the President wield his authority and stand by us so that we could do everything in our power to prevent the evil from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then you go on and say: "I spoke to General Pavao Miljavac too who briefly explained that the HV units were not committing any crimes." I think you testified yesterday that he was one of the commanders, one of the Generals in charge of Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He was one of the two generals. I think the other was General Miljavac who was in the Main Staff alternatively leading the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The meeting with him took place on the same day that you had the meeting with Jarnjak and Valentic or the day after?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all of that took place on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By the way, where did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With General Miljavac, I can't remember. We would meet often both in the Ministry of Defence and in the foreign affairs ministry. But as to that particular meeting, I really can't remember now. I can't say where exactly. With Jarnjak it was in the government of the Republic of Croatia. With Valentic in his own office within the government buildings. With the President, we walked around and were stoic in our discussions, because I was hard hit by this and wanted to depict to the President just how serious the situation was and what we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he told you one of the commanding Generals or Generals in charge at the end of August that the HV units were not committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that you believed him, because you received similar information from the field. Now, what information did you receive from the field?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information to the effect that various gangs wearing uniforms and out of uniform were looting, setting fire to houses, looting property, and that individual crimes were being committed. So that was the information that reached me at that point in time and that the scale of those crimes was greater than I had previously believed or knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you be specific. Can you tell me who the person was or the report that came from the field and made you confirm what you got from General Miljavac?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from -- well, one of them, for example, was the President of the Helsinki Watch, Mr. Zvonimir Cicak who told me that. Then there was Peter Galbraith who also told me that. Then there were several other respectable journalists who told me that they had information that the scale was grater. So those were the three basic sources and, of course, then it was all confirmed by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But are you saying that these sources you mentioned Mr. Cicak from the Helsinki Federation, Mr. Galbraith confirmed that the scale of crimes was greater, or did they also confirm that the HV wasn't committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me that the Croatian Army was committing crimes, nobody at all. Mostly it was said that people in uniforms were seen but not that the Croatian Army itself was committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then you met with Mr. Susak. And that's at the bottom of page 10 in English, and in Croatian, page 12. Now, here you say, and I quote: "Susak knew about the crimes, but he also denied that the men under his control were responsible. All he says was: Mate, it is not being done by the regular army." Do you remember the meeting with Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the office before lunch, in the presidential palace. He said, Mate, those things are not being done by the regular army, and then I said what Jarnjak had told me, that it was necessary to free the area of the army of the soldiers and the Home Guard units, that is to say, the non-professional units. And then he said that he was carrying out an enormous demobilisation withdrawing the army. When I say enormous demobilisation, that means almost 190.000 in the space of two months, although I can't give you the exact figures, and I think from 190.000 it was reduced to less than 50.000, and so he said that many soldiers had already left for operations together with BiH army and the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he also said that it was -- that great evil was being done but he said that it was wasn't being done by the regular army, by the regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just in terms of context, and I noted that Mr. Waespi skipped over a portion that's related to this, but this is at the top of the page, which I think may have some relevance and provide context to the bottom of the page that we're getting into now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm happy to read what whatever context counsel think is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Minister -- if counsel refers to the comment from Mr. Jarnjak: "Minister of the Interior Jarnjak confirmed all the information I had. I asked what we could do to stop lawlessness and killings. He suggested that police should immediately be given control of that area in which anyone could wander as they please. The Croatian Army was transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina and practically there was no authority to control the situation in the liberated areas." Now your meeting with Susak and the other meetings you mentioned Mr. Jarnjak, did they place -- take place before or after you had received the letter from German Foreign Minister Kinkel?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which happened later? The letter or the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the -- well, Minister Kinkel's letter came before and then the talks took place. So it was a warning to me, and I took it seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then on page 11 in English, you say that -- or you write that: "Shocked by the received information but also by Tudjman's and Susak's lack of power to urgently stop the crimes, I decided to take a sharp media approach. And you talk about the interview given to Globus in which you explicitly condemned chaos, delinquency, and so on. Do you remember when you gave the interview to Globus?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recently talked to the journalist. I had a briefing with them, not an interview. And I asked -- well, I had a briefing, not an interview and that was around the 1st of September, sometime around there. I can't say exactly when. Now, as far as the question goes, or, rather, the relationship towards this, both President Tudjman and Susak and Valentic and Jarnjak, all of them condemned the crime, but I wanted to have this crime stopped immediately. Immediately. And I considered that if, on the Croatian side, the media were to write about this, that this would help us stop the crimes from taking place. And I did this a number of times during my lifetime, and I was successful. I went to the media and spoke up publicly about certain things that I considered to be good, and that the Croatian public should know about, and that they would be then be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. Let's move on to a related but slightly different topic. That's the international reaction to these crimes. And I think you testified that you received, in the aftermath of the operation on the 7th of August, concerns by the international community. You were talking about ethnic cleansing was -- was raised and so on. That was on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I have to say is that, as far as ethnic cleansing is concerned, I rejected it equally energetically as I do know. My position in relation to it remains absolutely the same. Why? Ethnic cleansing did not take place. The rebel Serbs or the local Serbs, as we called them, in a planned way, encouraged by their leaders, moved out of Croatia. Of course, there were those among them who were -- who left out of fear and fearing revenge and there was revenge, and because of -- the indoctrination that they had been subjected to ever since 1987. So my position remains the same as it was on the 7th of August: There had been no ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you received a number of communications, either letter or phone calls from the foreign minister of UK, Mr. Rifkind, Susanna Agnelli, foreign minister of Italy, all raising concerns abut what was happening. That was on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move forward to the 24th of August. This letter of Mr. Kinkel has been discussed here a couple of times or a number of times. Do you remember having received, actually, the letter of Mr. Kinkel?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember receiving it. And I remember speaking with Minister Kinkel before receiving the letter and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could have P2660, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you: The letter, would it still be available?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you still have the letter of Mr. Kinkel?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do have it in my archive, but the -- no, I'm not referring to my personal archive. I'm referring to the archive of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and it must surely be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report in a German newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung which you might know. And they report about the fact that Mr. Kinkel wrote you that letter. And please read briefly the article for yourself, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. Is that a fair report about the letter of Dr. Kinkel that received you [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more or less accurate. I don't remember every single detail any longer. But he warned me about the arson, looting, and the killing of cattle. He also warned me that the international or the European community would be negative in reacting to that because at that point the European community had suspended the negotiations for trades and co-operation agreement, and this is what the letter was roughly about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at the same time, you met with the Austrian Chancellor Vranitzky, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have 65 ter 7482, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I can already read from a Reuters report titled: Vranitzky warns Croatia to respect human rights, dated 24th of August. "Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky warned Croatia on Friday to respect human rights saying it was a prerequisite for closer ties with the European Union. Vranitzky who held talks with Croatia foreign minister Mate Granic called on Zagreb to investigate and punish all human rights violations in the Krajina region. Refugees and UN observers have spoken of widespread looting, burning, and abuse of civilians during Croatia's recapture of the Krajina from Serbs who had seized control of the region during Zagreb's 1991 war of independence from federal Yugoslavia." And then talks about 150.000 Serbs who fled. Vranitzky demanded access for international observers to all areas where alleged human rights observations had been reported. Mr. Granic told reporters in Vienna on Thursday that Zagreb would invite human rights organisations and international observers to investigate claims of atrocities. He insisted, however, that the Croatian Army had not been involved in any violations. He said: "Any Croat civilians found to have committed human rights abuse would be brought to justice." And then there's a reference to the article of Mr. Kinkel in a German newspaper. Can you confirm, Dr. Granic, this report as accurate?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more or less accurate. It is accurate in so far as indicating that Chancellor Vranitzky warned me about the information that reached at least Austria of the criminal activities taking place on the ground. That's number one. Number two, he requested that we grant access to international observers on which score I agreed with him, and I proposed on my return to Zagreb to President Tudjman that all observers whoever sought access to go to Croatia, be given access, and this was the fact. We granted them access, and we also said that we would punish the perpetrators, and I said yesterday that at least 3.000 persons had been processed in relation to the events that took place in the aftermath of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Access to the observers, was that from day one, or were they reacted in additional days and maybe also later? Or are you claiming that there was never any restriction to access?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was restricted only in -- in the course of the first three days of the operation, whereupon it was granted forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And here we're on the 24th of August, it's still your belief at that time that the Croatian Army had not been involved in any violations. That's your knowledge at that time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Mr. Prosecutor. My knowledge at the time was that the Croatian Army had not done as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at the -- a couple of exhibits talking about crimes by the HV, and you were shown a few already this morning by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender 65 ter 7482, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2666 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to show to the witness, Mr. President, P1133.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this, Dr. Granic, is dated 6th of August, 1995. It's a daily report. It comes from Colonel Ivan Zelic, from the Split Military District Command, and he reports to the chief of the political administration of the Ministry of Defence, Major-General Ivan Tolj. Do you know General Tolj?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know General Tolj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the Croatian version on page 2 and the English version on page 3, it talks about the entry of the units into the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Middle of page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "When our units entered the town of Knin we encountered around a thousand persons who had remained in Knin. Also encountered was an entire UNCRO crew in its base hospital and claiming that there was no water or medicines. They were seeking a way to get into the town. Because of the terrain clearing and for security of UNCRO members, they were not allowed to visit the town yesterday. The entry itself of our members and the treatment of civilians was proper and at the required level. However, the behaviour of our members regarding property found was catastrophic. Immediately after entry, the devastation of buildings and uncontrolled collection of war booty began, but military police units had already entered the town and manned the main check-points, preventing further destruction and devastation of property." You have never heard in the first two weeks after Operation Storm of the catastrophic behaviour of HV members when they entered Knin?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I'm seeing this document. I was not aware of it. As a minister, I spoke solely with my colleagues and with members of the Croatian government, in addition to the reports that I received, and it was on the basis of the reports that I was receiving, that I responded to my colleagues around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think General Miljavac, the commander of -- one of the commanders of the operation, would not have been aware of a report like that that was sent to the chief of the political administration of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had, and I still do have, absolute confidence in General Miljavac. What sort of reports he received is something I don't know. He told me what largely Minister Susak was telling me as well, and that was that the army was not committing crimes. Whether they meant by crimes killings in general or the killings of civilians, I don't know. I wrote about the things that I heard in my book, and this is the first time I've set my eyes on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the -- one of the documents you were shown this morning by Mr. Misetic, Prosecution Exhibit P918. Now, this is the warning by the office of the assistant commander for political affairs of the Split Military District. And it goes to all assistant commanders for political affairs. And if you look at the last page, you see it receives quite a wide distribution. You see, OG Sajkovic; OG Otric, OG Vrbanac, the commander of the Split Military District for information, again the chief of the police administration. This time, though, of the republic of Herceg-Bosna. Commander of the Knin garrison; again for information. 72nd Military Police Battalion and files. So a substantial list of addressees, would you agree with me, Dr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is an explicit warning, talking about the irresponsible behaviour of individual soldiers, NCOs, and officers who compromised the Croatian Army and state, and officers are lieutenants and above, of course, captains, whoever can be an officer?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've stated already this morning that it's the first time I have seen it. However, what I can say, in political terms, in other words, the conversations -- the daily conversations I had with President Tudjman and in the Croatian government all resulted in warnings to both the Croatian police and the army to prevent crimes from taking place on the ground. Of course, politically speaking the position to me was clear. Now, as for the actual activities of the police and the army and the way they operated, I was really not familiar with that at all, nor did any reports on this reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, the point I'm making, Dr. Granic, is this, and I'm not accusing of anything. Here we have a report, a warning on the 12th of August, 1995, that goes to a number of addressees. It talks in no unexplicit terms about killing of livestock, destruction, torching, it implicates soldiers, NCOs, officers. It even states that the possibility exists that the international community could undertake measures which would have unforeseeable consequences for our state. So this is a serious, serious warning that might affect Croatia. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Prosecutor. The only thing I can say is that, on a daily basis, daily, I warned the President and all the men -- ministers, and that nobody opposed my view. I had never experienced anyone opposing my position or the -- going against the warnings that I was receiving from all over the world, and I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think that it's conceivable that not only the letter we have seen before, dated 6th of August but also the letter now, the warning of 12th of August, could have escaped the attention, the knowledge of General Miljavac and Defence Minister Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object at this point. We've established -- if he wants to now show the book --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is being impeached here. We have the dates as to when his conversations were. That's been established as the end of August. And if we look at the book and see what is actually being discussed on that date, I'm not sure -- I think the witness is being mislead because there is an assumption in the question that hasn't been established in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, the point I'm making is that both Mr. Susak and General Miljavac knew that the HV was committing crimes and that they lied to the witness when they talked on the 24th or in the aftermath of the 24th of August. I would like the witness to explain how it was possible that he was given that information by these two Generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can he explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can he explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I wanted to put to him that he was lied to. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if someone doesn't speak the truth to me, could I explain not knowing that I'm not told the truth, just for the sake of argument, I'm using it, I'm not saying it was, but how could I explain what others moved to tell me what they told me if it is not the truth? Of course, you can ask but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my objection is something different. He is -- first of all, I believe the witness said that these discussions were on the 30th of August not the 24th of August. Secondly, again I'm hesitant in front of the witness, but the -- it hasn't been established that what was said on the 30th was that it never happened. The book says he is talking about what was happening at that point and that's why I had Mr. Waespi read the portion of the book at the top of the page as to where the Croatian Army was on the 30th of August. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness told us based on this book that he denied, that Mr. Susak told him, I'm not sure the witness committed himself to a date for the meeting, sometime after 24th of August, the end of August, that Mr. Susak then knew about the crimes but he also denied that the man under his control were responsible. And here we have a chain of documents showing with widespread distribution that Mr. Susak must have been appraised of that. And I want to ask the witness whether he can explain that maybe based on the conversations he had with Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, if we can just ask Mr. Waespi to point to the specific portions in the record where it has been established that the discussions about what happened from 4 August to that date of the meeting or whether what's being discussed is what is happening at the time they are speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing, Mr. Waespi, Mr. Misetic is seeking that you are very precise in dates and when quoting conversations or when referring to conversations. That, Mr. Misetic, is -- you're invited to do so that could avoid all kind of confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you talked about crimes, both -- or with all the interlocutors you had, Mr. Jarnjak, Mr. Valentic, Mr. Susak, were you talking about the specific period of time or just all the crimes that may have happened in the aftermath of Operation Storm until you had that conversation with Mr. Jarnjak, Mr. Susak, and Mr. Valentic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not specify. Of course, it all related to the situation in the aftermath of Storm up until that date. However, I have to say that my experience with General Miljavac had always been a positive one. Many matters that will probably come to the fore in this case were done by the two of us together. The same is true for Minister Susak. When we disagreed over certain matters he was not a man to lie. I don't know that he did lie about anything, even around the matters that we disagreed about which is only normal in a political party. So there was no reason for me to distrust him, not to believe what he said. Now, the point that I insisted on was that all of us, and especially those who had the political power, i.e., the minister of the interior, minister of defence who had the military police under him that they had to do everything in their power to stop the evil, and I was resolute on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, it's a good moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Waespi. We will have a break, and we will resume at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just add a couple of questions on -- on the topic we discussed before the break. Did you have an explanation why nobody informed you about these acts that we were talking about, you know, the continued torching, the killing of livestock as stated in P918, a warning that had a potential, you know, to -- for unforeseeable consequences for Croatia? Do you have an explanation that nobody would have informed you about -- about these acts?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that certain things were happening but not the scale of it all. The real scale of things, I received towards the end of August, information about that. Of course, I dealt in diplomacy. I had enormous diplomatic activities to get through, and I wasn't even in the daily round of the Croatian government affairs. And when I travelled, when I received information or heard about information like that, I acted in accordance with my conscious and acted promptly. And quite certainly people didn't like seeing things that happen, or knowing about things like that happen. And nobody opposed the general assessment made that it was very detrimental to Croatia itself and that it destroyed Croatia's credibility in the world and ultimately, in the final instance it was the destruction of Croatian property, of Serb citizens doesn't matter, Serb or Croatian, and that it would certainly have serious consequences for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When was it, for the first time, that you were told that the Croatian Army were committing crimes in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much, much later I heard that individuals were involved in certain events, but that was much later. Because, as I said, I devoted all my time to my diplomatic activities, negotiations and so on and so forth. And in fact, I was away from Croatia for quite a lot of time. So I exclusively dealt with diplomacy. We were dealing with peaceful reintegration, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Dayton Accords and negotiations. I was taken up with all that. So in physical terms, I didn't have time to go into any of that, nor was that my remit for me to engage in matters of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So is it fair to say you didn't really know much of what was happening on the ground, on a daily basis, because you were out, you know, being the foreign minister for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you said that you heard about individuals who were involved in certain events, my question to you was: When you were told about the Croatian Army committing crimes, that it was much later. If you can, tell me the month, the week, the day, when did you hear for the first time that members of the Croatian Army were committing war crimes in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that exactly. Quite simply, it was 15 years ago, after all, so it is impossible for me to reproduce when these things happened and be specific. All I can remember exactly are the meetings. I know when the meetings took place. But, otherwise, I really can't say, because I just don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. Let me move on to another aspect that, again, deals with your role in dealing with the internationals. Another theme of explanations by the Croatian authorities was the isolated nature of the crimes that were observed or noted by the international community, and I suggest to you, you just gave an example when you said a moment ago that you heard about individuals who were involved in certain events, a very vague expression, diplomatic, I take it. I'd like to show you 65 ter 4641. This is a report of the 27th of September, 1995, from your embassy in Geneva about the conversation with the German ambassador, Geert Ahrens. Do you remember Ambassador Ahrens?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was his role?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was, in 1991, the German ambassador who helped over the constitutional laws for the protection of minorities and later on he worked in the international -- well, he worked in Geneva and was a member of the conference -- the international conference on the establishment of peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think he also assisted over the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that went to you as well, as you can see from the last page, second page in Croatian. Now, you are quoted -- or I'm sorry. Ambassador Ahrens is quoted as follows on page 2 in the English and page 1 in the B/C/S. Ambassador Ahrens, he said that: "Everyday he reads reports from several sources which describe the situation in the former Sector South and North as very unfavorable. No one trusts Croatia anymore when it justifies its actions by saying whether they were isolated incidents or acts of frustrated refugees. There is an increasing number of indicators which prove that the matter involves intent and a well thought out policy. Houses are still torched, the property of Serbs is destroyed, and there are cases of extremely brutal murders. He asks what advantage Croatia might have to do this when it is more than obvious that most Serbs will not return." Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at it now, I'm beginning to remember, and I can say that this letter is certainly original. Would you like to hear my comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the beginning of September, there was a dramatic decrease in the number of incidents, and certainly the number reduced rapidly. However, as Geert Ahrens says, it is also certain that they still happened. Now he is asking whether this was a policy. It wasn't a policy, no policy at all, and I agree with his assessment when he says that it can only harm Croatia. That is absolutely true. It can just do harm. So anybody engaging in things like this, engaged in crimes not only against the property of those individuals, but it was a crime against Croatia itself. And that would be my assessment of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about the comments he made?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I would meet him from time to time, but I don't remember having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2667 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Dr. Granic, that you felt uncomfortable in your role as foreign minister of Croatia having to listen to the concerns and complaints of your colleagues at that time, reflected in this communication from your embassy in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I didn't feel comfortable, particularly since I shared that opinion in full, that every crime all looting and destruction not only was it immoral, but it was very detrimental to Croatia itself. And, of course, for my part, whenever I was sure that something was -- something untoward was happening, I wielded my influence, exerted my influence on the government and the President to do everything to stop that evil, and, ultimately, it was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me show you a comment by Ambassador Galbraith about your reaction vis-a-vis him about these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is P445 at paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I start reading from paragraph 13 of Mr. Galbraith's evidence: "With respect to his reference to the systematic destruction and looting of Serb homes," -- referred to in previous paragraphs -- "the witness" -- who is Ambassador Galbraith -- "explained that he was aware of this from many significant sources of information including his own observations and experiences, embassy officers, military contacts human rights groups, interviews with refugees or stragglers. UN officials, journalists, politicians, and some Croatian officials. With respect to the last, the witness noted that it did not come only from lower level officials but also from Foreign Minister Granic who told the witness on 13 October that he had not defended Croatia's conduct after Storm because he couldn't do that. He disapproved of what was happening in the Krajina and he wanted to the make sure the witness" -- Ambassador Galbraith -- "understood and didn't associate himself with it." Do you remember meeting Ambassador Galbraith on the 13th of October and having a conversation as remembered by Ambassador Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met every day or every other day with Ambassador Galbraith, so I can't remember the individual meetings, but the substance of it is correct. Not only that, I asked him to help. And so, at that point in time, every contribution in helping to stop what was going on in the field was valuable. Every contribution. All I can say is that I had support in the Croatian government in that respect, and I had support in the personage of the President of the Republic. He thought that things were exaggerated only to begin with and that it was the result of pressure from the international community. However, after our discussions at the end of September, he came to realize himself once and for all, that it was an enormous problem for Croatia and that it was very detrimental to Croatia. So my position was quite clear. Everything that was happening was harming not only the individuals to whom it was happening, but that it was harming Croatia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to another interview, public appearance you had, on 7th October, 1995. And it is reported by BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is 65 ter 7485.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And BBC reports an interview you gave to a Spanish newspaper. And the only incident I'm interested in, or the only part is the few last questions, and I'm reading it out. Perhaps there is no B/C/S translation, so we'll deliver that. "Turning to Krajina, do you agree that a soldier who steals cars is a poorly paid soldier from a banana republic? Your answer: "Our soldiers are very well trained and disciplined. They are some of the best professional soldiers in Europe. Following Operation Oluja, there were some incidents which I personally condemned severely: Thieving, houses burnt down, and killings carried out by individual civilians. We will thoroughly investigate these incidents and report to the international community. However, our army has been extraordinarily professional." Now, your comment about the extraordinarily professionality of the army, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two things: First, that the army executed the military part of the operation fantastically well, and secondly, that up until that time I didn't have any information about anything regarding the fact that the army had committed any crimes, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President, pending a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2668.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2668 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now here, Dr. Granic, we have the 5th of October, 1995, and you're still claiming that, at the time, you did not know that the members of the Croatian Army were committing crimes. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an interview that General Cermak gave in Slobodna Dalmacija, the same paper I think you gave an interview at the end of December 1995. And I'll read the relevant parts. "Cermak: There is no place for looters in the HV. "Knin, according to Colonel General Ivan Cermak, commander of the Knin garrison, a large-scale operation has been launched to resolve problems related to the illegal occupation of apartments and the looting and torching of homes, acts, regrettably, most often committed by members of the Croatian Army. Some ten warrants have already been issued for arresting and bringing before the military court in Split such soldiers, who, as General Cermak stated, defile the Croatian Army and have no place in it. "Referring to a text published in Slobodna Dalmacija under the headline, Apartment safari, General Cermak said that the claims in the text were completely accurate, but that military and civilian police units have been strengthened so as to prevent illegal actions. General Cermak also said that the commanders of the units whose troops commit criminal offences also bear responsibility. "However, the General added, there is no need for Croatian soldiers to forcibly move into apartments since the issue of solving their housing needs will be given priority." Now, this is, Dr. Granic, a month earlier, a public source, a newspaper, clearly stating that crimes are being committed most often by members of the Croatian Army. How can you, as the foreign minister of Croatia, still maintain a month after a publication like that, that the Croatian Army didn't commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What General Cermak says here, and he meant that people stormed apartments and looted, he probably knew about that better than I did. And I firmly believe him, if he confirms it, then it means it is correct. I also received information of that scope, saying that there was lack of discipline and that flats were being stormed and so on. That was common knowledge in Croatia, and people took over apartments. There was looting as well. But my answer there was when you asked me about crimes, I have in mind killings, murder, and so on. So up until that time, I didn't have any information about that, whereas information of this kind started to be given out in October or, rather, the end of September and October. They began to crop up in the media and became public. But not murders and killings. And as far as murders and killings are concerned, I had no information about that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think I asked you about killings and murders. I think I asked you about crimes. And you're not doubting that what's reported here, looting and torching of homes, these are crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. All of this is crimes. If you forcibly enter someone's house, if it is not your house. Yes, I agree. Torching is a crime, theft is a crime, looting is a crime. But one of the priority things, if you were to ask me, a foreign journalist, for example, were to ask me about crimes then they usually meant crime, killings committed by the Croatian Army, so that was what I had in mind when I gave my answers. That was the priority thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let me ask you again. If you remember, when was the first time you heard about crimes such as looting and torching of houses committed by the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information I got, as far as torching and looting is concerned that they were involved, I began to receive some time in September. I don't know exactly when. What we call rumours. The rumours began to reach me, that there was involvement in individual cases of the army too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So all of August and early September, despite the widespread nature of reporting of international monitors whom, you say, had unrestricted access, you have not heard of cases that members of the army, of the Croatian Army, were involved in looting and torching?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the reports, it always said that they were individuals in uniforms. That's how they put it. Uniforms. Not Croatian Army members. So I'm very precise and specific on that point. Now, of course, if nobody or if I received reports saying that it was not the army, and people in the field, various organisations that were there said that -- these crimes were perpetrated by people in uniform, in inverted commas, then I thought that these were criminal groups and that was true whether they were renegade soldiers or criminals or whether it was retaliation and retribution, there were all sorts of things, but it was -- the reference was always made to people in uniform, not the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could just check the interpretation on -- let me see. I heard -- I'm sorry, I heard renegade soldiers and I can't see it on the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you can't find it on the transcript, then, of course, it's -- would you like to have it in or that it is not correctly translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The latter, and I see the marks, let's -- for example at 128, line 14 if that's the right -- sorry, page 128, line 10 I think is where I heard, whether these were renegade soldiers. And if we could perhaps check that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said demobilized soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I'm trying to find the demobilized soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think at page 128, line 10 you will see a caret which I think the transcript will be corrected later as to that portion of the transcript, or it would have been added. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that he did say renegade soldiers because she thought she heard the witness say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's clear that it was understood to have been said, and the witness now said that he was talking about demobilized soldiers. And I'm always a bit confused by the page and line numbers, Mr. Misetic, because apparently I have a different page and line numbering compared to yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, you and I have the same pagination on our screens but on the centre LiveNote the pagination is different than what's on our individual stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now could you give us the context where that word, if you give the words before and the words after, where you -- where you think th at the word which now turns out to be demobilized appears so that we know where it should be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was after the phrase "criminal groups."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it still is not entirely clear to me. I see the "criminal groups" but where would then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will read out the context, Mr. President. I believe the witness was saying: I heard these crimes were perpetrated by people in uniform, in inverted commas, then I thought these were criminal groups, and I believe he said or whether they were demobilized soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that was true or whether they were demobilized soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you said when you explained that these crimes were reported to have been committed by persons in uniform, in inverted commas, did you there explain that these were either criminal groups or may have been demobilized soldiers? Is that ... You see you're nodding yes. That's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that I'm clear, when did you hear, if you recall, for the first time, that some members of army units were committing crimes? By crimes I mean, looting, burning, killing, torching?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I cannot remember that. It was 15 years ago. I can't remember a specific date. However, just as General Cermak said here, that there were instances were soldiers stormed apartments, that there was torching in individual cases where there were soldiers too. Yes. And I started receiving first information to that effect sometime in mid-September. That's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd like to show you P647, and I'm not sure whether you have seen the document before. This is a letter from you, Dr. Granic, to the chairman of the commission on human rights in Geneva. I think you might have been shown the document before. And it dates the 11th September, 1996; at least that's when it was faxed. Do you recall drafting this letter?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to have a good look at the document before I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, just to point out, Your Honour, the data on the faxed transmission is from 1996, not 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact I think the document is in -- I might have misspoken, I wanted to say 11 September 1996. And it clearly has to be after August, after 23rd August, 1996, because, in paragraph 1 we see a reference to an earlier communication. And frankly, Mr. President, I don't know where I have the date of 11/9/1996 from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But perhaps, Witness, once you have read the whole document, you can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the document itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean a hard copy because it might be difficult for you to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we either zoom in so that the witness is better able to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If could I see the top and the bottom part, as well. Which is the correct date of the letter then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's unknown. I believe we have heard from Elisabeth Rehn about this letter. So I take it that the information that I have, that the letter was written on the 11th of September, 1996 comes from her evidence. Do you remember anything more about this letter?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't remember. If I signed it, then it must be a letter of mine. But I don't recall it. You see, I was minister of foreign affairs for seven years during that difficult period, and I signed thousands of letters. I don't recall this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the third paragraph on the first page. "In this respect the Republic of Croatia has stated on several occasions that human rights violations occurred in the period immediately following the liberation and reintegration of those occupied territories. The perpetrators were individuals and groups, including some members of army units who were acting contrary to their explicitly written orders." I am interested in a couple of things here. Now you say that among the perpetrators were members of army units. Do you remember where you got this information from?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is indeed the date you told me, then this is absolutely the position that we held at the time. By that time, we had received sufficient information in order for me to be able to write a letter such as this one. The information I had came to me primarily from the Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Defence. This was official information. Some of the information came from the intelligence service. It was based on the -- it was this sort of information that I could use officially. Of course, as minister of foreign affairs, I received a great deal of information from ambassadors, international organisations. I read the press, and whenever I wrote something officially, that reflected my actual position, my actual view.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it took you or your office quite a while to come to the conclusion, assessment, that it's now "members of army groups" who were among the perpetrators over a year after the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not what the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not what the document says, and just because he said it at the time doesn't mean it wasn't said before. So I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is there another letter or another communication from your office saying that there were members of army units who were committing crimes that precedes this letter here?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, simply because it happened 15 years ago. However, what is absolutely beyond dispute is that, at the moment I knew this for a fact, I certainly shared my information with representatives of the international community who acted toward the Republic of Croatia as partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the term here --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies, if you want me to be even more precise than that, I can tell you that I most certainly shared my view with representatives of the American administration and the German administration. And we behaved equally toward the specialized agencies of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now the term here that: "The perpetrators including some members of the army units who were acting contrary to their explicitly written orders," what is the source of that? Who crafted this term?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I know that before Storm an explicit order was issued not to violate the Geneva Conventions governing the laws and customs of war. This letter was drafted by excellent diplomats, by professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the reference I just quoted relates to explicit orders or an explicit order that was issued before Operation Storm started. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this one order. However, the meetings we had in the government I remember two things that can easily be proven. One of them is the -- a meeting of the government or at least two meetings of the government, where we issued explicit orders to the effect that there should be no violations of international conventions and that the army and the police should do everything in their power to bring to justice those who were offenders or to prevent them or when there was the crime concerning Varivode. So these are at least three cases involving the government, and there were discussions with the President of the Republic where I'm sure following these discussions the President took steps because of course it was only the president who had powers over the army and he acted upon it and took measures. So, none of these professionals would have drafted something of the sort had they not had something to substantiate it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your letter. For me, it suggests that these individuals were acting contrary to their explicitly written orders, which, I think, are orders issued to them, individually written. Am I wrongly understanding this phrase here?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they were issued to them individually. The orders applied to all members of the Croatian Army and the police. That's what I meant. I did not mean that they were individually issued to them. I wouldn't know about any such individual orders. It was the duty of the commanders to implement the orders, and how they executed them, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And the last issue in this letter I'm interested in is just the next sentence thereafter: "For objective reasons the Croatian authorities were unable to prevent a certain number of criminal acts perpetrated by individuals and small groups not under its control?" Can explain me what your -- I think you said extremely intelligent diplomats meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away, they were excellent diplomats and they had experienced the war from its earlier days ever since the aggression on Croatia. However, criminal groups are one matter, and, as I said previously, demobilized soldiers are quite another. Those who, at that point in time, were not members of the Croatian Army. And, of course, there were such cases, and this is what we had in mind in referring to it in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I'm not clear, and I'm starting to get a little bit tired. Did I ask you what is it meant by "for objective reasons?" I'm interested in that term. What are these objective reasons that --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vastness of the area that had been liberated, which was sparsely populated. The movement of great numbers of the Croatian Army, almost 200.000 of them. There were criminal groups which felt that their time had come. There was also the revenge taken by Croatian displaced persons, expelled persons who were going back to their homes and found them burnt down, destroyed, or on fire. Then the demobilized soldiers who were from the area, great numbers of people moving through the area and those were the reason. The territory was vast and difficult to control because it constituted almost 20 per cent of the Croatian territory. That's what was meant here. Of course, this does not justify a single crime that was committed. However, I have to state what the objective circumstances were, where attempts were made to prevent such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But these objective reasons don't take away the responsibility of the commander to control his units so they don't commit crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the military component of it, of course, as far as the army is concerned, every soldier is responsible to his commander, and I don't think we need to discuss that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the other way around as well: The commander for the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The commander is responsible for his soldiers and needs to make sure that the proper procedure is carried out where one of his soldiers is responsible for something like that. This is why the military police is there. As I said, there can be no justification for any such act. But, Mr. Prosecutor, as an individual who was minister of foreign affairs and who can be a bystander and a -- look at it as an observer because I wasn't part of the army or the police, you see that over there, space of several days, 20 per cent of the Croatian territory was liberated, and, of course, that was the target for all the individuals or groups to engage in looting. In addition to this, I said that there were those who engaged in taking revenge for what had happened to them previously. And you could see that's where a Croatian village had been burned, the neighbouring Serb village would soon thereafter burn as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me read the next sentence, which allows me to move on to the next topic. It says here in P647: "However, in all cases, where it was established that the crime had been committed, the competent government bodies undertook actions provided for by law to duly prosecute and punish the perpetrators." That's an overstatement, isn't it, in all cases?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the cases -- well, quite certainly one can't say that it was the case for all the case -- the cases that happened. But certainly in all the cases that the government was aware of, and where investigations were carried out. And, as I said, there were 3.000 such cases, or I'm no longer sure whether it was 3.000 cases, 4.000 individuals, or 4.000 cases and 3.000 individuals. I think that the latter is true that were tried. In other words, whatever the government and its agencies were aware of, that's what was processed. Now, whether there was full resolution at the time, well, certain issues could be raised. I thought that this should have been done more radically and energetically. If you ask the minister of the interior he would tell you that he did everything in his power. He personally always -- I personally always was for resolute steps to be taken in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter 4792. Mr. President, that's an excerpt, a page from a book by Ivo Josipovic The Hague Implementing Criminal Law, Zagreb, 2000. And we have disclosed certainly the whole chapter to the Defence, and the book is certainly available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivo Josipovic is, Dr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know Dr. Ivo Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you I apologise for the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can you briefly explain who Dr. Josipovic is.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a professor of international law. He is politically active today as well. He is the presidential candidate of the SDP. However, as far as international law is concerned, I appointed him at the proposal of my associates a liaison officer for the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So he is a respected lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's go to the -- I hope this is the next page or the page thereafter. We might have uploaded the table of contents as well, but I'm only interested in the one page with text. If we can move on. Yes, that's the page in Croatian. And the next one in English. And in English, it's on the top of the page. Let me read out what's said here about the topping [sic] and then about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This book obviously talks about cooperation between Croatia and The Hague. "On behalf of IDS, member of parliaments, Damir -- member of parliament Damir Kajn said: "I find the hubbub which has been raised about the Tribunal in The Hague and the alleged summons of Croatian Generals to The Hague absolutely unnecessary, damaging, and on the verge of the political ratio." He added: "The only sensible thing which has happened over the past three months within the ranks of the ruling establishment was the speech delivered by Minister Granic who spoke openly about how Croatian justice had not shown enough determination and perseverance in prosecuting crimes committed in liberated territories, especially after Operation Oluja. "He said that the Croatian people could not be defended by protecting perpetrators of crimes and we were all aware of the unwarranted destruction of thousands upon thousands of houses after Oluja and the criminal killing of 450 elderly males and females." And it goes on to talk about numerous crimes against Croatians. Slobodan Milosevic. Mr. Granic, is that an accurate quote, as far as your comments in the Croatian parliament is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
