utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could break down the quotes so that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I asked the witness about -- as it relates to him. But I can -- I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you, before footnote 243, those five lines, "the only sensible thing until Operation Oluja." Do you remember having delivered a speech, speaking about how the Croatian justice had not shown enough determination and perseverance in prosecuting crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this here, it is not clear to me when -- what Mr. Ivo Josipovic is referring to. I know one thing, and that is that when the constitutional law on co-operation with The Hague Tribunal was passed on behalf of the government I spoke in the Croatian Assembly or Sabor and I put forward the law. I proposed the law in conformity with President Tudjman, the government, and the top echelons of state government. And in proposing this law I expounded why we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- bent on passing it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Waespi apparently wants to know whether these are your words. So if would you please focus your answer on whether written or spoken, whether the quote reflects your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the quote is from Damir Kajn from a member of parliament, and perhaps I can give some context because it is on the previous page. The parliamentary session, do we understand it, in which Damir Kajn made that quoted was in February 1999, so the speech delivered by minister Granic to which Mr. Kajn refers having happened over the past three months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I missed that, Mr. Waespi. Nevertheless, the quote apparently is used to reflect what Mr. Granic said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you wanted to the find out -- no, let me see -- no, the quote is from -- let me just see. "The only sensible thing" -- and that's footnote 243, I think. That's a quote of what Mr. Kajn said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Mr. President. So my question to the witness would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you make a speech in late 1998, in which you said that the Croatian justice had not shown enough determination and perseverance in prosecuting crimes committed in liberated territories, especially after Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you would like to know is whether Mr. Granic ever delivered a speech in which he used the words, as in this book, Mr. Kajn is quoted as having spoken them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just be very precise here because I sense there may be some confusion, and I want to make sure there isn't. We're only talking -- attributing the quote of the portion of a sentence that begins: "After Minister Granic" -- the words Mr. Granic spoke openly about -- the question is whether the rest of that sentence is something he said, not the rest of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For the time being, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I ... Could you phrase the question in such a way that it's even understandable for me, Mr. Waespi, which perhaps requires a lot of skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure I'm up to it at this moment. But I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand it is difficult. Could I assist you. You have read this quote of what Mr. Kajn said, and in this quote he refers to a speech delivered by you, Mr. Granic, in which he says that you would have spoken openly about how Croatian justice had not shown enough determination and perseverance in prosecuting crimes committed in liberated territories especially after Operation Oluja. Now, do you remember that you ever delivered a speech in which you used this language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember a speech in 1996, when I proposed the constitutional law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. And -- well, I remember that. Now, this is a free interpretation of my words. My positions were that the Croatian judiciary should have been far more resolute in prosecuting people for crimes committed after Oluja. And yesterday in response to Defence counsel I said that quite certainly what was happening with the abolition and reducing the number with amnesty and people in Eastern Slavonia and so on, was not stimulating for justice and the judiciary. I was in favour of more resolute steps, more resolute action. Now I don't know about this figure. I don't think I stated a figure at all, but I certainly did say that the Croatian people were not -- would not be defending themselves but defending the perpetrators of crimes and that there was unnecessary destruction and unnecessary killings of elderly men and women, for example. Varivode being an example in point. That was certainly my view, but I didn't -- I don't remember having mentioned any figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have now dealt with the -- several portions of the quote. Mr. Waespi, I am aware that I may have contributed to the confusion. Apologies for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you be more specific. What should have the judiciary done differently?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that the judiciary prosecuted 3.000 individuals later. But when I say more resolute, I want to see more speed, more speed in prosecuting. Regardless of the fact that it was very difficult when you had Slobodan Milosevic on the one hand and everything he did, and Karadzic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth, but I personally always strove for greater resoluteness on the part of the judiciary to act. Of course, the political powers can't influence the judiciary but they do have the right to state their political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you thought that was lacking from within the judiciary that resoluteness in addressing the crimes that occurred after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judiciary in Croatia has progressed immensely and can conduct all trials with great competence, and I believe that the judiciary in Croatia is on a par with the strictest European standards, and this is best borne out by the fact that The Hague Tribunal has given over certain cases to Croatia, and I think that Croatia now at the high levels and at the various centre, district centres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I do understand that you praise the present quality of the Croatian judiciary, but that's not what Mr. Waespi asked you to tell us about. Although I also can understand that you ask yourself whether you have to tell us again. I do understand that Mr. Waespi wanted -- was seeking your confirmation that you thought that the judiciary had not been resolute enough in addressing the crimes after Operation Storm. I think that is what you said already; but if I misunderstood you, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the date is mid-1998, if that's the time we're referring to then it was my position that the judiciary should be more resolute. Not that it didn't prosecute, it did. It prosecuted a large number of cases, and there is a separate book written about that, all the cases that were prosecuted, but I considered that they should be even more decisive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2669.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to go to P2616, which is a document, I believe, we have seen today or yesterday. It's the minutes from the Council for Co-operation with the ICTY, dated 6 November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which is about the time-frame you were just mentioning. Now I think we are already aware who is present here. Ministers of justice and defence; you as the foreign minister; and various topics are discussed; ICJ proceedings, ICTY. And I would like to get to a comment you made on page 3 in English, and also in Croatian. And you discuss these proposals I think by Mr. Rifkind whom you mentioned, I believe, this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in both -- in -- page 3 in both versions, please. I hope it's the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's P2616. Yes. That's the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll read out the relevant part. "Dr. Granic, said that, in his opinion, all the proposals seemed bad from a political point of view. Two points are important in this respect. First of all, prior to the Oluja operation, a part of our territory was occupied, which was confirmed by the UN resolutions [sic]. This UN resolution represented the first global battle that was won by the Croatian diplomacy, and it also confirmed that Yugoslavia was responsible for the occupation. Therefore, the fact that there was an occupation and that some areas were occupied is indisputable. Second of all, in defining the Oluja operation, we ourselves called it a military and police operation. So, it was a planned operation and it was executed as planned. Our shortcomings surfaced subsequently after the Oluja operation, when we have not processed possible perpetrators of war crimes." Do you stand by that comment here? Is that what you said during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said at that meeting. That's what I said in the Assembly. That's what I said publicly. Because I considered that there should be even greater resolve in prosecuting those who had committed any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the statement is fairly straightforward. We have not processed possible perpetrators of war crimes. It's not qualified, not enough, or should be more. It is fairly straightforward, you would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, it's not true that we didn't prosecute anyone. That's absolutely not true. That thesis is not true. Now, when I spoke at this meeting, I had first and foremost in mind what I'm telling you here and now and what I said publicly at the time. We needed a higher degree of resolve in prosecuting. Not that we didn't. 3.000 people were prosecuted. 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these -- the figure of 3.000 prosecuted, I think you also said 4.000 crimes. You mentioned these figures a number of times. You don't really know the details.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you don't know the details, who the perpetrators are, what the crimes were they were prosecuted for, whether there were just criminal reports filed or convictions. You don't know the details of this rough figure, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I don't know the details. Although I think that before 2000, that is to say, 1999 a book was published about all that. But, of course, it wasn't my job at the time. That's not what I dealt with. I didn't deal in the justice system. It wasn't my job to deal with -- I was speaking as the vice-premier and foreign minister and somebody who was from the top political echelons, and I gave political assessments. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, nevertheless, Mr. Waespi, ask a few more questions? This number of 3 or 4.000 comes back several times in your testimony. Now would that cover Croat suspects and Serb suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It encompasses everyone, both Serbs and Croats after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be my next question. Not -- you're not referring to crimes committed between 1991 and 1995 but only crimes that were committed after the first days of August 1995. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it would encompass only crimes committed in -- well, let's say in Sector South, that area, or would it be a broader territorial area, which was covered by these 3 or 4.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That number refers to events after Oluja, in the area that was liberated. But it also -- but it encompasses, as I said, both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea about what percentage of cases was brought against Serbs and what percentage of cases was brought against Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the details, Your Honour, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not an approximate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I can't say, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the number which apparently is important for you because you mentioned it several time, do you -- what's the source of -- of this approximate number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Government of the Republic of Croatia, and the then-Ministry of Justice, which gathered that information, and I'm sure you will have at least one witness coming in who will be able to address the details. I can't speak of the details, and I heard the figure from the government of the Republic of Croatia, and it was a figure that was bandied about publicly in the media. And I heard it at an official government session, a Croatian government session, and of course, that includes all crimes from the less serious to the most serious. That is to say, including looting, torching, and that kind of thing right up to killings and murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, although we have no trial chamber following -- I'm moving to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can deal with it in approximately four minutes, that's fine. I would rather avoid going too far beyond 7.00, one or two minutes, no problem, but not more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, it's -- the next topic about the return of the Serbs, and I think we some more time than four minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps if you're confident that we could still stick to the schedule tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I -- I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. Then I think that we should adjourn for the day. Mr. Mikulicic, any further need to discuss with Mr. Granic any of the lately disclosed document, because my instructions to him will depend on your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you. We don't have such demands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Granic, I now instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. No exceptions this time, so you are supposed not even to speak with the Markac Defence anymore on these matters. And we will adjourn and resume tomorrow, Friday, the 20th of November, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
